article_text:
A group of talent agencies and producers have joined forces to create to the American Entertainment Alliance dedicated to promoting U.S. independent production. The new coalition will push for legislation requiring major studios and streamers to allocate half of their original content budgets to indie production.

Founding members include CAA , WME , UTA , Anonymous Content, Blumhouse, CAA, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer’s Imagine Entertainment, Jeff Sagansky, Legendary Entertainment, MRC, Peter Chernin’s North Road, Producers United, Propagate Content and Ziffren Brittenham.

Related Stories

Ex-UTA Agent Dante DeSario, Investor Michael Lambert Launch Collage, A Management Firm For AI Production

CAA Signs 'The White Lotus' Season 4 Cast Member Caleb Jonte Edwards

The AEI is focused on strengthening competition, expanding opportunities for indie producers and creators, and supporting film and TV production in the U.S., addressing a fundamental restructuring of the entertainment business. Studio consolidation and streaming have dramatically narrowed the market for independent content, disrupting the economics of film and TV, said UTA on Instagram today, noting it’s “proud to be a member of the American Entertainment Alliance”

The AEA will advocate for “modern creative ownership rules that reflect today’s streaming marketplace” and support policies that make the U.S. more competitive as a production destination.

Watch on Deadline

The number of original television series has fallen dramatically in recent years from what in hindsight has been dubbed ”peak TV” and consolidation in the industry has deeply rattled the industry, none more than the $110-billion merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that closed last week.

The giant company now called Skydance Media made some commitments to the indie film space i n a settlement with a group of Attorneys General who had sued to block the merger. They include a promise that four films a year from the combined studios’ slate will be independent, defined in this case as based on an original screenplay or co-produced by Paramount. Paramount must also establish a $25 million Independent Film Fund ($5 million per year for five years) specifically designated to acquire and fund indie films.

Likewise, the idea behind the new Alliance is that forcing Hollywood’s biggest players to source a big chunk of content from outside would reenergize the market.

“As film and television increasingly consolidate, we need a regulatory framework that puts creators first, protects industry workers and preserves competition,” said UTA Vice Chair Jay Sures.

The Alliance was first reported in the New York Times.

The group’s push in Washington, D.C. would follow key legislation introduced last month providing the first ever federal tax credit for U.S. production, which could be layered on top of state incentives. It’s not clear if or how or it will move ahead but a group of bipartisan legislators sponsoring the measure is hoping to pass it by January, likely attached to a spending bill later this fall.

Sympachy》", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "东京歌剧城艺术画廊于10月17日起举办“种子与根基——都市的耕耘方式”展。我们采访了开幕前一日举行的媒体预览会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
東京オペラシティ アートギャラリーで 10 月 17 日から、「種と根っこ ― 都市の耕し方」が始まりました。開幕前日に行われた内覧会を取材しました。

本展は、現代美術、建築、ファッションの３分野から、それぞれ総勢 10 名の作家が参加しています。作家たちは今日的な問題に向き合いながら植物や自然環境に関わる作品を制作しました。私たちが直面している異常気象、温暖化など深刻な問題に限らず、食べたり、排泄したり、まとったり、住んだりといった、各作家が日々行っている身近なところから、それぞれの仕方で自然を把握し、つながろうとする作品が展開されています。

本展を担当した３人のキュレーターを代表して、能勢陽子さんは「『種と根っこ』というタイトルには、人間の移動とか、その過程での変容、また自らのアイデンティティやルーツ、そして創造の種がどのように根付き展開していくのかという意味が込められています。都市のただ中にいながら、人間も自然の一部であり、様々なやり方で、またその感覚を取り戻せるというふうなことを感じていただけると幸いです」と話しました。 では、気になった作家の作品と言葉をいくつか紹介していってみましょう。

最初は浅野友理子さんです。いろんな土地を訪れて、その土地の植物をきっかけに、人や虫なども含めて見えてくる色々な物語や、その土地で受け継がれるものをテーマにしています。今回の新作《落果の営み》ではオペラシティ前の街路に植わっているヤマモモを題材としました。鮮やかなヤマモモの実がアスファルトの地面に落ちて、道行く人たちに踏まれた様子を描きました。実際は果汁が通行人の服や道を汚してしまうため、ヤマモモの実は早めに剪定されてしまうので、この場では実際に見られない光景です。浅野さんは「グレーのコンクリートの地面に本来落ちるはずだったヤマモモの染みというという敬遠されるものを、とにかく美しく描きたかった」と話します。そのほか、鳥が消化できずに吐き出したペリットから芽を出した植物などを描いた作品もありました。

続いては、今村文さんです。壁に貼られたのは、押し花のように見えますが、水彩で描いたものを切り取ってコラージュした作品です。実在する花にも見えますが、基本的には空想の花です。手前のインスタレーションは、温かい家の裏庭というイメージで、外の世界とつながって広がって行くイメージを表しています。

ほかに二つの花が重なり合っている絵も展示されています。植物が隣り合って、自生していると、知らないうちに絡まり合って、一つの植物になっているような時があります。「人と人も隣り合って、一緒に住んでいたり、一緒に仕事していたりとかすると、その人のことが好きになったりも、嫌いになったりもいろいろあるけれど、その人が消えた瞬間に何か自分の中に痛みのようなものを感じるのは、知らないうちに根を絡み合っていた感覚があるんじゃないか」と思って制作したそうです。

普段は、毛糸を使ったタペストリーのような作品を制作する 䑓原 蓉子さんは、小さい時から編み物をするのがルーティーンになっていて、編んでいるうちに精神が安定してくるそうです。今回は出産したばかりで大きな作品に取り組む時間がなく、ニョロニョロとした細長い編み物を新作として毎日つくり続けました。編んだものは１か月ごとに並べて展示されています。精神状態が安定すると編む長さが短くなったり、気持ちが荒ぶっている時は編み目がきつくなったりするなど、日々の精神状態が日記のように作品に表れます。色は自分が食べた玉ねぎの皮を煮出して染めています。こちらも煮出す量や時間で色が変化し、日々の微妙な心や生活の変化が可視化されています。

鈴木初音さんは、自分が食べるために育てたキクイモの茎から繊維を取りだし、粉砕して乾かしたものに、はんだごてで焦がして絵を描くなど、「（作物を育てるなど）私が生きていることと、絵を描くことが地続きになっている部分をすごく大事に思っています」といいます。今回は水辺をイメージして場所を作りました。そのきっかけは、「私は都心にいても、地下鉄脇の通路の水たまりに小さなエビとか微生物が泳いでいるのを見つけ、どんな場所でも水があったらそこに生き物が生まれるということに衝撃を受けた」からだそうです。メインの作品は、岐阜県に滞在中に、家の裏にあった湿地にいたオタマジャクシが育ち、どんどん水の中に手足を伸ばしていく様子がどこか根っこに感じられたことからインスピレーションを受けたそうです。

ファッションデザイナーの山縣良和さんは、９月から開催している前橋国際芸術祭にも参加し、そちらでも行列をテーマにしたインスタレーションを展開しています。子どもがトイレの前に人形を並べて遊ぶ姿をみたことをきっかけに、行列を人間の根源的な営みとみなし、おもちゃや彫像を並べた行列のなかに様々な場面を取り入れています。

今回は子どもから大人になっていく過程のほか、止まらない戦争なども表現されています。最も目を引くのは仏教絵画の「九相図」からイマジネーションをえた《 Where the story ends― つづくよ つづくよ》。展示室にそびえ立つランウェイを、骸骨が空に向かって並んでいます。作家の出身地である鳥取砂丘の砂がまぶされた骸骨には花が生けられ、死と再生を表しています。

展示室外には子どもの成長を願うつるし雛をモチーフとした《ここに いても いい Bittersweet Sympachy 》も展示されています。

このほかにも意欲的な作品同士が呼応、調和し、響きながら魅力的な展示空間を形作っていますので、ゆっくり時間をかけて見て回ることをお勧めします。参加10作家のプロフィールなどはプレビュー記事をご覧ください。（美術展ナビ編集班・若水浩）

title_original: Direzione pittura: intervista a Adelisa Selimbašić
editorial_title_zh: 走向绘画：对阿德利萨·塞利巴希奇（Adelisa Selimbašić）的专访
editorial_excerpt_zh: 与这位将身体从其自身具象中解放出来的艺术家面对面，在色彩之池与将目光移向边缘的构图之间，模糊性成为了一种自由的形式。文章“走向绘画：对阿德利萨·塞利巴希奇（Adelisa Selimbašić）的专访”源自……

"是谁说出了关于“绘画之死”的最后定论？在全意大利的工作室里，一股年轻艺术家浪潮正在证明事实恰恰相反，他们将古典传统融入我们这个时代的超连接想象之中。这个全新专栏致力于介绍活跃在美丽国度的年轻画家。通过对他们创作幕后的直接、无滤镜采访，我们将去发掘那些选择用世界上最古老的媒介来讲述当下复杂性的艺术家的痴迷与语言越界，这延续了对肖像、风景和静物等传统流派的重新定义。我们采访了阿德利萨·塞利巴希奇（Adelisa article_text:
Chi l’ha proferita l’ultima parola sulla “morte della pittura”? Negli atelier di tutta Italia, una wave di giovani artisti sta dimostrando l’esatto contrario, innestando la tradizione classica all’immaginario iper-connesso dei nostri giorni. Questa nuova rubrica è dedicata ai pittori emergenti attivi nel Bel Paese. Attraverso interviste dirette e senza filtri dietro le quinte della loro ricerca, andiamo a scoprire le ossessioni, gli sconfinamenti linguistici di chi ha scelto il medium più antico del mondo per raccontare la complessità del presente, nel solco di una ridefinizione dei generi tradizionali, dal ritratto al paesaggio e alla natura morta. Abbiamo incontrato Adelisa Selimbašić (Karlsruhe, 1996), qui la nostra intervista.

Come descriveresti oggi, in poche righe, la tua ricerca pittorica?

«Il mio focus, momentaneamente, è soprattutto sulla ricerca della forma, legata, in questo caso, al corpo. Questo viene visto come una superficie modellata dalla luce, quasi come un atto scultoreo, che poi, sulla tela, viene descritto attraverso il colore e la linea, tramite ampie campiture, quasi come se fossero piscine di colori. Questi elementi tendono quasi ad astrarre il corpo, a liberarlo dalla sua stessa figurazione. Il corpo non è più motivo di narrazione, ma diventa protagonista in sé, di fatto, del lavoro.»

Come ti sei avvicinata alla pittura?

«Mi sono resa conto che era la cosa che più amavo fare e per la quale provavo estremo piacere. Posso stare a dipingere per ore senza mai avere il desiderio di fermarmi.»

Quali sono gli artisti e maestri del passato che senti come riferimenti o punti di ispirazione? E tra i contemporanei, chi segui con maggiore interesse?

«Tra i maestri del passato, sicuramente Michelangelo, Caravaggio e Artemisia Gentileschi. Tra i nomi contemporanei, Marlene Dumas, Miriam Cahn, Nan Goldin… per citarne alcuni.»

La pittura per te è un fine o un mezzo?

«Non la considero né un mezzo né un fine, penso che le due cose coincidano nel mio lavoro.»

Quali temi affronti nel tuo lavoro e perché li ritieni importanti in questo momento?

«La libertà del nudo, la sessualità vissuta come innocenza, l’ambiguità come possibilità di non essere definiti e classificati, e l’identità sono alcuni dei temi che tratto all’interno del mio lavoro. Sono temi che considero importanti da affrontare, soprattutto perché viviamo in una società che tende a etichettarci e a inserirci all’interno di categorie da sistemare in scatole e poi riporre su degli scaffali. Penso sia importante, oggi più che mai, lasciare spazio all’empatia e alla possibilità di riconoscersi nel diverso, nell’altro.»

Quali elementi consideri fondamentali nel tuo modo di dipingere (ad esempio colore, segno, composizione, materia, tecnica)?

«Sicuramente la composizione è una grande protagonista. Mi diverte lavorare soprattutto sui bordi della tela, togliendo l’attenzione dal centro e portandola maggiormente verso i margini, là dove solitamente non dovrebbe esserci nulla di interessante. Attraverso il colore e la luce ricerco la profondità.»

Quanto influisce il contesto contemporaneo (sociale, culturale o politico) sul tuo lavoro?

«Il contesto nel quale si sviluppa il mio lavoro è estremamente importante per me. È proprio da questo che il mio lavoro trae ispirazione, ed è per questo motivo che mi sono spostata spesso e continuo a farlo.

Ogni città e ogni cultura che ho avuto modo di vivere mi hanno dato nuovi punti di vista e nuove direzioni verso cui rivolgere lo sguardo. Hanno aperto nuove interpretazioni di elementi che ormai erano stagnanti nella mia mente.»

Utilizzi strumenti digitali o intelligenza artificiale nel tuo processo creativo? Se sì, in che modo?

«Non utilizzo strumenti digitali o intelligenza artificiale.»

Quali influssi esterni alla pittura (per esempio cinema, musica, letteratura, immagini online, ecc.) sono più presenti nel tuo lavoro?

«A volte ho bisogno di evadere dall’eccesso di immagini a cui siamo esposti quotidianamente. Musica e letteratura mi permettono di allontanarmi temporaneamente da questa dimensione visiva per riattivare un’immaginazione più libera.»

Nel tuo lavoro quanto spazio hanno l’esperienza personale e quella collettiva?

«Penso che il mio lavoro parta spesso da un’esperienza o da una percezione personale, ma che poi questa si trasformi in qualcosa di più universale. Attraverso il corpo, l’identità, la sessualità e il modo in cui la società tende a etichettare le persone, cerco di affrontare temi che partono da me, ma che allo stesso tempo possono appartenere anche agli altri. In questo senso, l’esperienza personale diventa un punto di partenza per parlare di qualcosa di più ampio e collettivo.»

Durante la realizzazione di un’opera, qual è il momento che consideri più importante e come incide sul risultato finale?

«La scelta dell’immagine da rappresentare è per me un momento cardine per il risultato finale. Nella fase iniziale è proprio quest’ultima che andrà poi a incidere sulla dimensione del telaio, sul formato, sui colori, sull’atmosfera, sulla composizione, su tutto ciò che andrà poi a sviluppare il processo creativo.»

Quando decidi che un’opera è conclusa?

«Semplicemente lo sento. Guardo il lavoro e so che è concluso, e che ogni azione successiva andrebbe solo a forzare qualcosa che non è ancora lì.»

Cosa ti porta a scegliere la pittura oggi, nel contesto contemporaneo?

«La pittura è ancora oggi la pratica a cui amo di più dedicare il mio tempo.»

Pensi che il valore della tua opera possa variare all’interno di una grande mostra collettiva come Ensemble ? In che modo?

«Penso che sicuramente possa variare, perché un’opera, una volta inserita all’interno di una mostra collettiva, entra inevitabilmente in relazione con tutto ciò che la circonda e, soprattutto, con le diverse opere d’arte: il confronto può far emergere aspetti dell’opera che, vista singolarmente, magari non sarebbero così evidenti.»

article_text:
抗議活動を受けアート・バーゼル・パリが早期閉幕へ。美術館やギャラリーも相次ぎ臨時休業

10月24日に予定されている抗議活動を受け、25日まで開催予定だった アート・バーゼル・パリ が23日午後7時での閉幕を決定した。 フォンダシオン ルイ・ヴィトン や ガゴシアン も臨時休館・休業を発表しており、パリのアート界に影響が広がっている。

10月24日に予定されている抗議活動を受け、 アート・バーゼル・パリ や フォンダシオン ルイ・ヴィトン をはじめとする パリ 市内の美術施設やアートイベントが、休館や開催中止を相次いで発表した。25日までの開催を予定していたアート・バーゼル・パリは、24・25日の開催を中止し、23日午後7時（現地時間）をもって会期を終了する。

出展ギャラリーに宛てられたメールのなかで、 アート・バーゼル のチーフ・アーティスティック・オフィサーを務めるヴィンチェンツォ・デ・ベリスと、同フェアのディレクター、カリム・クリッパはこう述べている。

「今週末にパリ全域で懸念されるデモの状況、ならびに来場者の安全確保を考慮し、フェアは金曜日の午後7時をもって終了いたします」

コレクターや富裕層の多くは会期終了前にパリを離れるが、週末まで滞在する予定だったギャラリーのスタッフや美術関係者も多くいる。フェアの主催者側は、23日の閉幕まで展示を維持するよう出展ギャラリーに強く促すとともに、作品の安全な搬出を支援する方針を示した。また、「運営チームとギャラリー担当チームが、グラン・パレや物流業者、関係当局と緊密に連携し、会場への立ち入りや作品の搬出を円滑に進めるための計画を策定しています」と説明している。なお、ウィンストン・チャーチル通りで展開されているパブリック・プログラムの屋外インスタレーション作品については、別途撤去作業が行われるという。

このほか、実業家ギュスターヴ・ファイエのコレクション展を 開催している フォンダシオン ルイ・ヴィトンも、予防的措置として24日に臨時休館する予定だ。また、 ガゴシアン もパリの拠点を同日に臨時休業すると発表している。

US版ARTnewsがパリに拠点を置く複数のギャラリーに取材したところ、各ギャラリーは週末に臨時休業するかどうかを23日中に判断するという。一方、マレ地区で開催されているサテライトフェア「Post-Fair」は、デモを見越して24日の閉場時刻を午後1時に繰り上げることを決定した。同フェアの創設者であるクリス・シャープは、「出展者と作品の安全を最優先に考えた結果」と語っている。

早期閉幕の発表前、アート・バーゼル側はデモの影響について明言を避けていた。一方、参加アーティストのアリシア・クワデは10月21日、フェアのパブリック・プログラムの一環としてグラン・パレ屋外に展示されている自身の巨大な石の彫刻を、予定より早く撤去するとInstagramで 表明した 。クワデはデモに伴う「暴力」を非難し、「抗議行動自体は良いことだが、なぜすべてを破壊し尽くさなければならないのか理解に苦しみます。それでは自分たちの訴えを伝えることにはつながりません」と記している。

パリ市当局も24日に向けて警戒を強めている。「抗議活動とは無関係の暴徒による暴力行為が再び発生するおそれがある」として、市民に最大限の警戒を呼びかけ、同日正午以降はゴミ箱や自転車、カフェの屋外テーブルなどを屋内に移動させるよう推奨した。

抗議行動の発端は、10月17日、公立学校の予算不足などを背景に、拡大する社会的・経済的不平等を訴えた抗議デモで、フランス全土で行われ、50万人以上が参加した。この抗議活動は概ね平和的に行われたものの、一部では暴動や略奪が発生。デモは規模を縮小しながら翌18日まで続き、同様の抗議活動は他のヨーロッパ諸国にも広がっている。

フェアに参加したディーラーによると、運営側は警備を強化し、一部の来場者が参加を見送ったものの、フェアは早期閉幕の発表まで概ね予定通り進行していたという。しかし、ル・モンド紙は、こうしたアートフェアの華やかな光景と、その周囲に広がる社会的・経済的不平等との落差を 指摘している 。

ル・モンド紙がその一例として取り上げたのが、Instagramアカウント「 Documentations Art 」の投稿だ。同アカウントは、「アート・バーゼルは略奪のフェア」と題した投稿で、24日に会場のグラン・パレを「取り戻そう」と 呼びかけた 。同紙は、富裕層が投資や節税目的でアートを購入し、富を増やしていると主張するこの投稿について、不正確な情報や事実に反する記述が多いと批判している。一方、この投稿のコメント欄には、「24日には億万長者や大富豪たちはすでにパリを去っているだろう。当日会場を歩いているのは、何も買わない中産階級の来場者だけだ」という指摘もあった。（翻訳：編集部）

article_text:
Lehmann Maupin and Gallery Wendi Norris will collaborate on a two-part exhibition pairing the work of Surrealist artist Leonora Carrington and artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña for the first time.

The first part of the exhibition, titled “Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña,” will open at Lehmann Maupin in New York on November 19, while the second part will open at Gallery Wendi Norris in San Francisco in January. The two parts have distinct checklists, to accommodate for the different scale of each location, though the parts share some overlap.

Dealer Wendi Norris proposed the show to Rachel Lehmann, one of Lehmann Maupin’s cofounders, a few years ago. Lehmann was reminded of the conversation after visiting Vicuña’s solo show at the Irish Museum of Modern Art (IMMA) last November. (That exhibition was co-organized with Whitechapel Gallery in London, where a version of it opened last week.)

“Things sometimes take time until they sit in the right place,” said Lehmann, who reached out to Norris to see if she would still like to work on the exhibition. “One of the things we do is try to position our artists in different ways, and [it] became suddenly so obvious to me that I had missed out actually on something with Wendi.”

Norris began representing Carrington in 2004, seven years before the artist’s death in 2011 at 94. Over the years, she has placed Carrington’s work in intergenerational group exhibitions and staged reenactments of her plays, but this is Norris’s first show featuring both the Surrealist’s art and the work of a living contemporary artist.

“I love putting Leonora Carrington’s work in new context,” Norris told ARTnews . “I’m constantly trying to imagine how she would respond to things that we do, like this exhibition. One thing I feel I can say very certainly is that she would be overwhelmingly excited about an exhibition like this.”

The connection between Vicuña and Carrington extends back much further. In 1969, Vicuña, then in her early 20s, met Carrington in Mexico City while she was en route back to Chile after a trip to New York. In New York, Vicuña had “a vision [of] the painting that I needed to do,” she recalled. During that fateful meeting, which was explored in the IMMA exhibition, Carrington gave Vicuña advice that helped the young artist “transfer” what she saw to canvas, for a process she would call Calcomanías. “Carrington enables this transfer from the poetry of the very unusual or uncategorized forms into something which was very tangible, like a painting,” Lehmann said.

Norris added, “The exhibition, I think, will enable viewers to delve deeper into Carrington’s iconography and language, and the way it feels to read it, alongside Cecilia’s. I, for one, am excited to see what it will uncover. I don’t want to predict it because I’m excited about what I’m going to discover myself.”

The exhibition will feature new works by Vicuña alongside important historical ones by Carrington. In selecting which pieces to feature, the two galleries were guided by “the relationship that both artists had,” Lehmann said. “What has struck me most in speaking to Cecilia over the years was the influence that Carrington brought to her practice.”

One of Vicuña’s new paintings is Polvo del Sahara/ Saharan Desert Dust (2026), an underwater scene showing the light reflecting into the depths of the ocean, where a stone staircase leads to somewhere beyond the horizon. Lehmann hopes the exhibition will shed light not only on how Carrington’s influence will help us “to understand where Cecilia’s paintings are coming from,” but also on how “Cecilia continues Carrington’s legacy.”

Norris described the building of the checklists for each show as “an iterative process” that involved sharing images of potential works and their contexts over several months. “We were trying to think of Leonora’s love of the environment, her sense of humor, and her hybrid creatures and how that might speak to some of the similarities we see in Cecilia’s work,” Norris said, noting that after each proposal, she would ask: “How does that land with you and your audience?”

Norris has also thought about which of Carrington’s works to show in which venue, including showing two works that were included in her 1990 show at the Brewster Gallery and have not been shown in New York since. One is Eye Witness (1987), a wintry landscape of two figures who seem to look away from an apparition of sorts; a skyscraper in the distance bears a resemblance to the Empire State Building.

The two artists’ work has been featured in one recent exhibition, the 2022 Venice Biennale, whose title of “The Milk of Dreams” came from one of Carrington’s books. Vicuña was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement ahead of the Biennale’s opening. However, the two artists were featured in separate sections of the Biennale, so they were not positioned together, as they will be in this show.

Since the 2022 Biennale, Carrington’s work has also been seeing a revival lately, as it has been the subject of two traveling surveys, one that opened at the Palazzo Reale di Milano in 2025 and another that is currently on view at the Faro Santander in Spain. Beyond Carrington and Vicuña’s stylistic affinities, Lehmann and Norris pointed out how the reception of the artists’ work has changed over the decades and that both have only been canonized relatively recently.

“This has been a long time coming for artists like Leonora and Cecilia,” Norris said. “I think Leonora probably knew it was coming but was nonplussed about it. She knew she was planting seeds, and they were going to bear fruit one day.”

article_text:
Interview

Paul Pfeiffer on the Spectacle of Politics

“Perhaps the stadium is actually the replacement for the UN as a symbolic gathering point to conduct world politics,” the artist told Hyperallergic in an interview.

LOS ANGELES — In the early 1990s, Paul Pfeiffer began producing a series of striking interventions in found video footage, often featuring celebrated sports figures, to highlight the effects of media and fame on not just individuals but also the larger body politic. Using innovative post-production techniques, he removed key elements from scenes of professional boxers and basketball players, isolating them in various arenas, teasing out the uncanny undercurrents in such late modern spectacles.

Pfeiffer’s work further heightened the stakes of these scenes of pop culture by invoking art historical figures from classical sources, including caryatids from his eponymous 2003–4 series, and modern painting, as seen in his 1999 digital video installation “Fragment of a Crucifixion (after Francis Bacon).” He has also developed a wide-ranging practice of drawing and sculpture, as seen in his series of sculptural maquettes and imagined plans for a million-seat stadium, all named some version of Vitruvian Figure, and woodcarvings of pop singer Justin Bieber in the style of Jesus on the Cross — “Justin Bieber Legs Crucified (Seville)” from 2026 — which feature in his current exhibition at Galerie Perrotin in Los Angeles.

Hyperallergic: What do you think about the scaling up of mass culture in recent generations, and how it creates collective affects that can be appealing, but also lead to dystopian outcomes? I’m thinking of the quote, “A million Elvis fans can't be wrong” — would a billion Swifties gathering be a stadium too far?

Paul Pfeiffer: There's a proliferation of stadiums, often connected to cyclical events like the World Cup or the Olympics, traveling from city to city, such that the architecture mirrors this kind of rhythm.

If we think about soft power and the amount of politics conducted through the World Cup, and the listlessness and questionable effectiveness of the United Nations now, perhaps the stadium is actually the replacement for the UN as a symbolic gathering point to conduct world politics. It certainly hides as much as it reveals, but has become a staging ground for political pronouncements. In that way it’s beyond symbolic — the athletes' bodies move beyond the agonistic encounters in the stadium.

H: I think about Iranian athletes who trained outside the United States border during the World Cup due to the US government’s unwillingness to host them overnight, and faced this greater adversity just getting to their jobs. I think also of those people marching out of the UN assembly during Netanyahu’s speech, who voted with their bodies.

PP: For me, it's the play of the visible and the invisible, or the facade and the informal production scheme behind the facade. This is present in the ways politics are conducted through culture now, a formal symbolic aspect that carries a certain kind of weight. I agree about the spectacle of so many delegates walking out on Netanyahu is heartening — a bit of agency when we needed it.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025东京国际电影节将最高竞赛奖颁给一部历史史诗片，可以说是实至名归——这就是安妮玛丽·雅西尔（Annemarie Jacir）令人印象深刻的剧情片《巴勒斯坦36》（Palestine 36），影片扣人心弦地刻画了通往1937年英国提出分割巴勒斯坦提案、犹太定居者涌入以及巴勒斯坦抵抗运动兴起等一系列事件前的历史。本届电影节上，过去的身影无处不在，其中最显著的原因莫过于迎来了保罗·施拉德（Paul Schrader）1985年传记片《三岛：四部曲》（Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters）在长期缺席后姗姗来迟的日本首映。这部关于备受争议的右翼小说家三岛由纪夫的影片，在首映40年后才与日本观众见面。几十年来，尽管该片在世界各地屡获殊荣并已成邪典经典，但在日本的放映却一直被悄然阻挠——这很可能是因为施拉德曾遭到日本极右翼团体的强烈反弹，他们愤怒于一个美国人竟然在“亵渎”一位偶像。（有传言称，三岛的遗孀也曾表示反对，尤其是对片中暗示三岛据称存在的双性恋倾向的桥段。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《三岛：四部曲》在东京的迟到上映，恰逢三岛诞辰百年这一机缘巧合的时刻，引发了一场狂热（门票在10分钟内售罄），并折射出过去几十年间的文化变迁。而另一个（坦率地说有些刻意的）周年纪念，则为另一场备受争议的放映提供了由头：日本有史以来第一部长篇动画《桃太郎：海之神兵》（Momotaro: Sacred Sailors，1945）的4K修复版。这部片长74分钟、兼具无节制的军国主义宣传与开创性艺术造诣的作品，其放映是为了纪念二战结束80周年。该片于1944年由日本帝国海军委托制作，作为其战时宣传运动的一部分，由日本四大电影公司之一的松竹（Shochiku）动画师政冈宪三（Mitsuyo Seo）执导。影片将广受欢迎的民间传说英雄桃太郎——一个从桃子里诞生、双颊圆润、击败了一帮邪恶妖怪的小男孩——化作了一则意图明显的隐喻，影射日本对同盟国的军事努力及其在东南亚的帝国扩张。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在前半部分呈现出一种与迪士尼风格如出一辙的田园牧歌般景象、满是可爱动物在草地与河流间嬉戏之后，随着桃太郎成为一名军队将军、带领着成群的森林生物历经训练奔赴战场，影片发生了一次夸张的风格大转折。其中一个片段激情洋溢地刻画了日本对西里伯斯（Celebs，现为苏拉威西，属当今的印度尼西亚，片中被重命名为“果阿王国”）的入侵，将夺取当地荷兰殖民统治者的控制权包装成了一场光荣的解放行动。影片的结尾序列则是其最宏大的幻想飞跃。在日军战胜西方军队的对峙之后，桃太郎与一群漫画式的英国将军展开了谈判，这些将军的下巴随着他们对这个圆脸小男孩的恐惧日益加深而颤抖着——并最终妥协。这次放映证实了该片惊人的艺术造诣；其错综复杂的线条勾勒和极其流畅的运动轨迹令人目眩神迷，很容易让人联想到《幻想曲》（Fantasia，1940），海军省显然曾让政冈宪三观摩该片以作准备。考虑到与迪士尼动画师不同，政冈宪三是在极其有限的资源下工作的，甚至用酸清洗赛璐珞片（绘制动画所用的透明塑料薄片）以便循环利用，这一切就显得更加令人印象深刻了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，《桃太郎：海之神兵》背后的制作故事——以及其中包含的所有矛盾——才真正凸显了它的重要性。正如动画评论家乔纳森·克莱门特（Jonathan Clements）在其著作《神圣的水手：政冈宪三的生活与工作》（Sacred Sailors: The Life and Work of Seo Mitsuyo）中所写的那样，政冈宪三实际上是一名左翼活动家，曾在日本无产阶级电影同盟工作，直到警察搜查了他们的办公室，并将他和其他成员逮捕、虐待。由于当时艺术家对抗政府的机会日渐枯竭，他在绝望之中最终接下了制作《桃太郎》的工作。政冈宪三的动画团队不断因应征入伍而流失，最终不得不培训并雇用女服务员——她们的名字至今没有出现在演职人员名单中——来完成这部电影。该片的上映又是一场磨难，由于海军当局认为片中过多着墨于家庭生活而非战争场景，导致上映推迟了四个月；此外，首席动画师还被指控为“不爱国”的和平主义者。当《桃太郎: 海之神兵》于1945年4月登陆院线时，它已经成了一种修正主义叙事。不久之后，所有的素材都被认为已经丢失，很可能在空袭中被毁。但1983年，人们在一个仓库里发现了一份拷贝并对其进行了修复，这不仅让我们得以一窥日本动画的早期岁月，也让我们得以了解这些电影制作背后的工业和政治条件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《桃太郎：海之神兵》失而复得的传奇，与1985年的纪录片《山：袭击，再袭击》（Yama: Attack to Attack）形成了有趣的对照。这部纪录片是我在东京一个激进社区空间“Sawa Sawa House”的独立放映会上看到的。这部纪录片由活动家佐藤满夫（Mitsuo Sato）发起，旨在记录东京东部山谷（Sanya）社区日工的苦难生活。在那里，穷人、被遗弃者和外国人（其中许多是从日本殖民地抓来的强迫劳工的后代）遭到工厂老板与极道组织和警察勾结的剥削。正如佐藤在早期的画外音中所声明的那样，他的使命是坚称这些工人的日常生活值得被记录和保留——无论是在胶片中还是在生活中。在开机后不到一个月的时间里，佐藤就被极道成员刺杀身亡。由山冈强一（Kyoichi Yamaoka）领导的一群活动家决定完成这部电影；最终，山冈也遇害了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管如此，《山：进攻与反进攻》还是完成了，在过去的几十年里，“YAMA”放映及展览委员会一直在日本及世界各地零星放映该片，并且每次都会伴随映后讨论。影片从一开始就令人震惊：佐藤交代背景的画外音和镜头戛然而止，转而切入他尸体的特写镜头以及围绕其遇害展开的抗议集会。随后，影片以零散的章节展开，其中包括对劳动者的采访；记录他们生活和工作条件的影像，包括肮脏的街道和他们栖息的拥挤简陋旅社；以及他们公开痛斥工厂主和市政官员与黑手党勾连的惊心动魄的场景。尽管其碎片的结构是制作环境使然，《山：进攻与反进攻》依然让人联想起黑人音频电影集体（Black Audio Film Collective）的作品，尤其是他们于1986年创作、记录黑人和棕色人种反抗伯明翰警察暴行的影像肖像《汉兹沃斯之歌》（Handsworth Songs）。在这两部电影中，对不公的深切愤怒化为了一种表现主义的视听诗学；两部作品都坚持不将拍摄对象呈现为受害者，而是将其展现为掌控自己生活的主体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《山：进攻与反进攻》强调了一个事实：记录并放大被压迫者抗争的工作不能仅靠事后追忆——它必须是当下正在进行的过程。正是这种责任感，推动了我在东京当代单元中极为喜爱的一部作品诞生：藤元明绪的《失落之地》（Lost Land），该片入选了聚焦日本导演新作的“日本电影现状”（Nippon Cinema Now）单元。藤元明绪曾在缅甸生活和工作多年，他着手填补媒体对当前针对罗兴亚人的种族灭绝及其引发的难民危机报道的空白——至关重要的是，该片是与那些经历过这些可怕灾难并幸存下来的罗兴亚剧组人员和演员合作完成的。影片开场讲述了一对年幼的兄妹及其姑姑正准备经由水路和丛林开启一段艰难的旅程，最终抵达马来西亚。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从早期的场景来看，我本以为自己在看一部纪录片——摄影机贴得很近且采用手持拍摄，对话自然得令人不安——这使得片中孩子们被冷酷的蛇头赶上一艘简陋的小船、只能靠配给的零星食物度日并被遗弃在偏远海岸的场景看起来分外揪心。随后，一个伴随着感伤弦乐的场景暗示这是一部精心雕琢的剧情片，为我提供了一丝勉强的喘息之机。在整部影片中，它以真实性的承诺将你拉入其世界，随后又用温和的戏剧性修饰将你拉出——这种摇摆让我不禁思考：我们如何利用剧情片将自己与现实隔绝，又如何利用纪录片让我们将现实视作共情的前提。尽管这部电影包含戏剧化演绎，但从它所描绘的事件很可能就在我们继续生活的同时于此时此刻上演的意义上来说，它无疑是真实的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于性侵这一棘手主题的电影，往往为了囊括那些本难以尽述的经历，而流于模式化或老生常谈。《在他们的足迹中》之所以脱颖而出，在于它拒绝提供确定性的答案和圆满的结局。该片由日本电影人小田香掌镜，具有令人惊叹的视觉细腻感。摄影机驻足于双手、双脚和各种物件之上，并玩味着对焦与景深，使我们得以贴近银幕上的人们，却又从未让我们获得一幅全貌，以免我们自以为在他们全部的复杂性上真正了解了他们。在影片的叙事中，生存并非一场有终点的旅程，而是一种每时每刻、日复一日的交涉；虐待也不是一种无法逾越、将人与世隔绝的经历，而是交织在共同创伤着这个世界的众多紧密相连的暴力（父权制、监狱、贫困、战争）中的一种。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
It was fitting that the top competition prize at the 2025 Tokyo International Film Festival went to a period epic— Palestine 36 , Annemarie Jacir’s impressively mounted dramatic account of events leading up to the 1937 British proposal to partition Palestine, the arrival of Jewish settlers, and the emergence of the Palestinian resistance movement. The past loomed large at this year’s edition, not least because the festival hosted the long-overdue Japanese premiere of Paul Schrader’s 1985 biopic Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters , about the controversial right-wing novelist Yukio Mishima, 40 years after its initial release. For decades, even as the film garnered awards and achieved cult status around the world, screenings in Japan were quietly blocked—likely due to the backlash Schrader had faced from Japanese ultranationalist groups enraged that an American was “desecrating” an icon. (Rumor has it that Mishima’s widow also had objections, particularly to allusions to Mishima’s purported bisexuality.)

The belated arrival of Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters in Tokyo, timed serendipitously to the centennial of Mishima’s birth, created a frenzy (tickets were sold out in 10 minutes) and reflected the cultural shifts of the intervening decades. A different (and frankly contrived) anniversary provided the rationale for another controversial screening: a 4K restoration of the first-ever animated feature made in Japan, the 74-minute Momotaro: Sacred Sailors (1945), a piece of unbridled military propaganda and pioneering artistry, screened to mark 80 years since the end of World War II. The movie was commissioned in 1944 by the Imperial Japanese Navy as part of its wartime propaganda campaign, and it was directed by animator Mitsuyo Seo at Shochiku, one of Japan’s Big Four studios. The film deploys the popular folktale hero Momotaro—a chubby-cheeked boy, born from a peach, who defeats a band of evil ogres—as a not-so-veiled metaphor for Japan’s military efforts against the Allied Powers and its imperial conquests in Southeast Asia.

Following an incongruously idyllic, Disney-inspired first half involving cutesy animals frolicking in meadows and rivers, the film takes a bombastic turn when Momotaro becomes an army general, leading cadres of forest creatures through training and into battle. One section offers a rousing account of Japan’s invasion of Celebes (now Sulawesi, part of modern-day Indonesia, and here renamed the “Kingdom of Goa”), framing its takeover from the island’s Dutch colonial rulers as an act of glorious liberation. The film’s concluding sequence is its most grandiose flight of fantasy. After a confrontation in which Japanese forces prevail over Western armies, Momotaro engages in a negotiation with caricaturish British generals whose jowls jiggle as they grow increasingly intimidated by the round-faced little boy—and finally give in. The screening confirmed the film’s incredible artistry; its intricate line drawings and exceedingly fluid movements are hypnotic to watch, recalling Fantasia (1940), which the Naval Ministry apparently showed Seo in preparation. It’s all the more impressive given that, unlike Disney artists, Seo worked with extremely limited resources, hand-washing the cels (transparent celluloid sheets on which the animation is drawn) with acid in order to reuse them.

It is, however, the story behind Momotaro: Sacred Sailor ’s production—and all the contradictions involved—that underlines its significance. As animation critic Jonathan Clements writes in his book Sacred Sailors: The Life and Work of Seo Mitsuyo , Seo was actually a left-wing activist who had worked with the Proletarian Film League of Japan before the police ransacked their office, and arrested and tortured him and other members. He wound up working on Momotaro in a moment of desperation, as opportunities for artists going against the government were drying up. Seo kept losing his animation crew to the draft, and ultimately had to train and employ waitresses—who remain uncredited—to finish the movie. The film’s release was another ordeal, delayed by four months because the Naval authorities felt that it dwelled too much on scenes of homelife as opposed to war; further, the lead animator was accused of being an “unpatriotic” pacifist. By the time Momotaro: Sacred Sailors hit theaters in April 1945, it was already a revisionist narrative. Not long after, all materials were believed to be lost, likely destroyed during air raids. But a print was discovered in a warehouse in 1983 and restored, allowing us not only a glimpse at Japanese animation’s early days, but also the industrial and political conditions under which these films were made.

The saga of the loss and rediscovery of Momotaro: Sacred Sailors offered an interesting counterpoint to the 1985 documentary Yama: Attack to Attack , which I caught at an independent screening at Sawa Sawa House, a radical community space in Tokyo. The documentary was begun by activist Mitsuo Sato to chronicle the struggles of the day laborers of Sanya, a neighborhood in East Tokyo, where the poor, outcasts, and foreigners (many of them descendants of forced laborers brought from Japanese colonies) were exploited by factory owners in collaboration with the yakuza and the police. As Sato declares in his voiceover early on, his mission was to assert that the everyday existence of these workers was worthy of preserving—both on film and in life. Less than a month after he began production, Sato was stabbed to death by the yakuza. A collective of activists, headed by Kyoichi Yamaoka, decided to finish the film; eventually, Yamaoka was also murdered.

Nevertheless, Yama: Attack to Attack was completed, and for the last several decades it has been presented occasionally in Japan and throughout the world by the “YAMA” Screening and Exhibition Committee, always accompanied by a discussion. The film is shocking right from the beginning, when Sato’s scene-setting and narration is cut short by close-up footage of his dead body and the protest rallying around it. It then unfolds in jagged chapters that feature interviews with laborers; portraits of their living and working conditions, including the squalid streets and overcrowded hostels where they sleep; and thrilling scenes of them publicly berating factory owners and municipal officials over their connections to the mafia. Though its fragmentation is a product of the circumstances of its production, Yama: Attack to Attack evokes the work of the Black Audio Film Collective, particularly Handsworth Songs , their 1986 portrait of Black and brown folks’ resistance to police brutality in Birmingham. In both films, a deeply felt rage against injustice manifests as a kind of expressionist audiovisual poetry; and both insist on presenting their subjects not as victims, but as self-determining agents of their own lives.

Yama: Attack to Attack underlines the fact that the work of recording and amplifying the struggles of the oppressed cannot happen only in retrospect—it has to be an ongoing process in the present. This responsibility propels one of my favorites from among the contemporary selections at Tokyo: Akio Fujimoto’s Lost Land , which screened in the “Nippon Cinema Now” section for new works by Japanese directors. Having lived and worked in Myanmar for several years, Fujimoto set out to address the lacunae in media coverage of the current genocide against the Rohingyas and the resulting refugee crisis—crucially, in collaboration with Rohingya crew and cast members who have survived those terrible experiences. The film opens with two young siblings and their aunt preparing to make an arduous journey, via boat and through jungles, to reach Malaysia.

I assumed, from the early scenes, that I was watching a documentary—the cinematography is close and handheld, and the dialogue unnervingly naturalistic—which made the scenes of the kids being herded onto a flimsy boat by ruthless smugglers, fed rationed bits of food, and abandoned on remote coasts gutting to view. Then a scene, scored with sentimental string music, suggested that this was a carefully calibrated fiction, offering me a tenuous bit of reprieve. Throughout, the film draws you into its world with the promise of authenticity, before gentle dramatic flourishes pull you out—an oscillation that made me wonder about the use of fiction to insulate us from reality, and of documentary to make us demand reality as a prerequisite for empathy. Even though the film involved dramatizations, it is of course real in the sense that it depicts events that are likely unfolding at this very moment, while we go on with our lives.

Another highlight of Nippon Cinema Now, In Their Traces by Shigeru Kobayashi, also pondered the task of empathy and cinema’s role in it. The documentary opens with a phone call between the director and his friend, an older woman, who continues to be plagued by flashbacks to being raped as a child and abandoned by her mother. Against images of green fields passing by the windows of a train, we hear their conversation in voiceover: she is in pain and wants to end her life; he struggles to hold the frightening weight of her hurt. From there on, Kobayashi accumulates a portrait of survivors of abuse navigating its aftermath. There’s a photographer who takes evocative pictures of (and with) other survivors, and works with a group of offenders as her means of processing her experiences. Another woman runs a “free school” for young victims where they can experience a safe environment and rebuild their sense of trust. Halfway through, Kobayashi reveals that he, too, has a personal connection to the subject matter—after suffering abuse at the hands of a father scarred by World War II, he ran away from home and was adopted by another family.

Films about the tricky subject of sexual assault can be schematic or platitudinous in an attempt to contain what are, often, uncontainable experiences. In Their Traces stands out for its refusal of certainties and resolutions. The film is lensed by Japanese filmmaker Kaori Oda and has an incredible visual delicacy. The camera dwells on hands, feet, and objects, and plays with focus and depth of field, to bring us close to the people on screen without ever allowing us a complete picture, lest we assume we know them in their full complexity. In the film’s telling, survival is not a journey with a destination, but a moment-to-moment, day-to-day negotiation; and abuse is not an insurmountable, isolating experience, but one of the many interconnected violences—patriarchy, prison, poverty, war—that scar the world we all share.
excerpt_original: Past imperfect: many of the highlights of the festival reflected on how we remember troubled pasts

article_text:
News

Mamdani Begins Reconstruction of Historic Chinatown Building Decimated in 2020 Fire

Some $184 million will go toward the revival of 70 Mulberry Street, which once housed community-based organizations.

On Monday, November 9, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, along with the commissioners for the departments of design and construction, citywide administrative services, and cultural affairs, commenced the $184 million reconstruction project of 70 Mulberry Street, a historically significant building that sustained severe damage from a fire in 2020.

Upon the project's expected completion in 2030, 70 Mulberry Street will house or provide additional space for the five community organizations that operated there before the fire, including the Museum of Chinese in America (MOCA). The new building will include artist Jennifer Wen Ma's "Wings of Everchange 易之翼," a permanent, three-part art installation commissioned by the Department of Cultural Affairs’ (DCLA) Percent for Art program .

Working between Beijing and New York City, Ma has produced varied interdisciplinary media ranging from " cleansing walks ," which appear like one-person funerary processions, to collections of plants coated in Chinese ink.

" Wings of Everchange 易之翼" in the 70 Mulberry Street space (courtesy Department of Cultural Affairs)

Designed by Grimshaw Architects, the new building retains architectural traces of the 1892 building, while expanding to include six community rooms, multipurpose areas, outdoor spaces, and several modern accommodations. The renovated building is expected to provide approximately 30% more public space than the original facility and will extend three floors higher.

Founded and constructed in 1892 as Public School 23, the building was repurposed into a community hub in the mid-1970s. After the fire devastated much of the building's structure in 2020, the five organizations operating there relocated to nearby venues. While MOCA had moved to its 215 Centre Street flagship in 2009, it retained the old gallery space at 70 Mulberry Street as an archival space and research library for the museum's 85,000-item collection, most of which was salvaged from the fire.

Since accepting a $35 million city capital grant tied to the construction of a Chinatown jail in 2019 , MOCA has come under intense scrutiny. In July, protesters condemned museum leaders for accepting the so-called "jail money" in exchange for their complicity in the jail's construction and the possible devastation to Chinatown's communities.

Ma's public installation touches upon much of the Mulberry Street site's historical record and its role in Chinatown in three capacities.

The central sculpture in the building's atrium will be modeled after the graceful brushstrokes of Chinese calligraphy and incorporates salvaged materials from the 2020 fire. Within the sculpture, glass orbs serve as time capsules dedicated to certain individuals or groups touched by 70 Mulberry Street. Ma also plans to launch a publicly accessible website and app with oral testimonies from 70 community members about the building. The third part of the installation extends to the historic spiral stairwell, where ink paintings on glass panels snake up several floors along the inner stair tower.

The New York City Public Design Commission unanimously approved Ma's design in January 2024 as part of the Percent for Art program, which mandates that 1% of eligible funds for city-backed construction projects be spent on public artworks.

"Our community has gone through so many challenges and changes," Ma said in a statement. "I set out to make a work that would embrace these changes, honoring our history, anchoring us in the present and taking us soaring into the future.”

article_text:
As Netflix debuted the first trailer this week for Greta Gerwig ‘s Narnia : The Magician’s Nephew , fans were treated to an iconic needle drop.

Gerwig recently explained how she was able to convince Led Zeppelin to let her license “ Stairway to Heaven ” for the feature adaptation of C.S. Lewis’ prequel book, after the band has notoriously shot down all previous requests to feature the 1971 song on screen.

“I showed them and I talked to them, Robert Plant and Jimmy Page, and I was so moved that they allowed me to use the song,” Gerwig told Stephen Colbert at a Q&A . “They did it because they saw the heart of the story in the film and they too love C.S. Lewis, and they have a reverence for his work. The whole thing was very fortuitous. But I’m so happy that it got to be this song.”

Related Stories

First Trailer For Greta Gerwig’s ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’ Teases Punk Rock Multiverse & Cosmic Creation Of Aslan

Greta Gerwig On Why She Chose Meryl Streep To Voice Aslan In ‘Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew’

Gerwig explained that the song was “exactly the story” of the movie. “It’s an epic song. It’s an amazing song. It’s a narrative. It’s about a spiritual journey,” she said.

Watch on Deadline

“It’s about the true path of enlightenment and spirituality, and then this path of false idols and the wrong roads you can go down,” added Gerwig. “And I was like, ‘This is exactly the story of this movie.’ It really is a spiritual quest and a spiritual journey, so to me, this was the song that made sense to introduce this into the world. But this song, they had not let it be used in anything.”

Previous failed attempts to license “Stairway to Heaven” include a 1995 episode of The Simpsons , Almost Famous (2000) and last year’s Stranger Things finale, while Mike Myers poked fun at the band’s protectiveness of the track in a scene from Wayne’s World (1992).

Premiering Feb. 12, 2027 in Imax before its April 2 Netflix debut, Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew follows two children Digory (David McKenna) and Polly (Beatrice Campbell) as they explore the office of Digory’s Uncle Andrew (Daniel Craig) and end up in a magical wood filled with pools that lead to other worlds. One pool takes them to a dead city, where they awaken its queen (Emma Mackey) who exterminated its population, accidentally setting her loose on London.

The organization of the 2027 World Press Photo Contest shares that it will be introducing the World Press Photo Nature Award and the World Press Photo Sports Award .

These awards create dedicated space to recognize outstanding nature and sports photography from around the world. Three awards in each field will be selected by the jury from Singles and Stories entries submitted across all regions, celebrating stories that explore our relationships with the natural world and the human, cultural and social dimensions of sport.

article_text:
Interview

Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“The crisis is the system that we’re in,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning data journalist and artist says in an interview with Hyperallegic about her first book, “Ten Lives.”

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections , the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026).

When I met her in the West Village in September, she’d just come from recording its accompanying audiobook, a delicate process given the visuals on its pages. Chalabi organized meticulous interviews conducted with anonymous subjects across income levels over the course of six years into 10 vividly fleshed-out characters. Each represents a particular economic class, illustrated in her signature hand-drawn style and punctuated by reflections on her own financial struggles as a young journalist and, more recently, in the wake of her mother’s illness. Chalabi carries a long tradition of data visualization — W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes comes to mind — into her refreshing candor about class and the stifling silence around it, particularly in journalism and the art world.

That insistence on specificity and honesty in her reporting goes hand-in-hand with her political advocacy; Chalabi donated her $15,000 Pulitzer Prize award to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate and has been fighting for Palestinian rights since she was a teenager. Her drive to seek out and represent truth, in Ten Lives and in her social media posts, is anchored in a sensitivity and profound sense of responsibility. In this way, she restores some of the humanity and dignity to the statistics that capture the brutality of genocide, exploitation, and economic inequality, one brushstroke at a time. In an interview, we spoke about the financial realities of journalism, the value of collaboration in an era of isolation, and the art and literature that sustains her. Our conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Hyperallergic: In the intro to Ten Lives , you recall getting scolded for not observing “the etiquette of looking away” as a child. And it’s so striking that you have made a career of doing the opposite. How did you decide to make class, something we’re taught to overlook from a young age, the subject of this book?

Mona Chalabi: The first line of the original manuscript said, “I wrote this book because I was paid a shitload of money to write it.”

H: Ha!

MC: And my editor was like, “Yeah, you can't do that. No one's gonna want to read a book that you wrote simply for money.” But I also knew that this was a commercial idea, and that did inform it. I have been quite shameless about the fact that I want my work to reach a wide audience. That has always, always mattered to me. It was the beginning of the pandemic, and part of the way that I pitched it was this idea that there's gonna be a big financial crisis and the dynamics are more nuanced than simply talking about the one percent. There's this idea of a coming economic collapse or a coming financial crisis. But as soon as we're in it, it's not this cyclical model. The crisis is the system that we're in that is so broken.

H: That gradation of class that usually doesn't get talked about is such a crucial contribution of this book. What led you to stratify these stories based on subcategories that often just get collapsed into “working class, middle class, upper class”?

MC: Class is really informative about who I am and how I move through the world and my relationships. And I felt like it was really, really lacking in our discourse. I feel a bit hesitant to use the word “discourse,” but it's just true. And it's not just about discourse, it's more mundane than that. It's the way that someone like me can say, “I'm an Arab, cis, heterosexual woman,” with total ease, but class doesn't really come into it. There's a dishonesty there. Actually, class is really, really important. And many of us aren't really talking about that in accurate and fruitful ways.

article_text:
自画像 47KMのダンス

劇場公開日： 2026年11月9日

解説・あらすじ

父親の故郷である中国湖北省の村に10年以上通い続け、村の記憶と自身の変化を記録してきたジャン・モンチー監督による「自画像 47KM」シリーズの第2作。村で亡くなった人々のための記念碑を建てようとする日々を追った。 2010年、大学を出たばかりのジャン・モンチーは、老人たちにインタビューをしようと「47KM村」と呼ばれる村を訪れ、村を襲った飢餓の記憶を聞き取り始める。約1年ぶりに村へ戻ってきた監督は、村で亡くなり忘れ去られようとしている人々のために記念碑を建てようと考える。反対の声を受けながらも1軒ずつ家を訪ね、賛同と寄付を募っていくが、詳しい聞き取りを重ねるうち、人々の証言が大きく食い違っていることに気づいていく。 監督のジャン・モンチーは1987年、中国湖北省生まれ。中央民族大学でダンスを学び、ダンサー、振付家として活動しながらドキュメンタリー制作を始めた。山形国際ドキュメンタリー映画祭が共催する「47KMシリーズ特集上映」（2026年11月7～20日＝ポレポレ東中野）でシリーズ全10本とともに上映され、本作は日本初上映となる。

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good morning!

A major work by Gustav Klimt will go under the hammer at Christie’s New York next month with a price tag of $60 to $80 million.

Celebrated Indian artist Jogen Chowdhury died in Kolkata on October 25 at 87.

The National Gallery Singapore’s chief curator Patrick Flores and assistant chief executiveChris Lee, are the latest to depart the institution in December amid a staff shake-up.

The Headlines

KLIMT IS COMING . A major work by Gustav Klimt will go under the hammer at Christie’s New York next month with a price tag of $60 to $80 million, and it’s guaranteed to sell, reports ARTnews . If sold on November 17th, Klimt’s lush, green landscape painting Litzlbergkeller (1915-1916), which has been in the same private collection for nearly three decades, would put it among the Austrian artist’s top prices at public sale. The current, unnamed owner paid $14.7 million for it at Sotheby’s in 1997, which is the equivalent of $30.9 million today. “The inn of Litzlbergkeller sits at the water’s edge, between Klimt’s allover technique and abstraction, form and dissolution, prewar and certainties and the unknown,” said Max Carter , global chairman of 20th and 21st century art. Klimt’s current auction record is for Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914-16), sold at Sotheby’s, New York in November 2025 for $236.4 million.

IN MEMORIAM . One of India’s most celebrated artists, Jogen Chowdhury, died in Kolkata at 87, reports The New Indian Express . He had been ill with a rare type of blood cancer, according to his family. Trained at the Government College of Art & Craft from 1955 to 1960 and later at the École Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris in the 1960s, he was among a second generation of postcolonial artists who reshaped contemporary art in India. “Chowdhury’s rich contributions in the field of art are evident in numerous government buildings … The works he left behind will remain for centuries,” said West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari. Known for his figurative expressionist works, often using a cross-hatching technique to distort the human body, Chowdhury blended Western modern artistic currents with local Indian influences. In the 1960s and 1970s, “many of our major artists were fond of doing abstract art, thinking that it was ‘Modern’ and the ultimate expression of art,” Chowdhury told The Punch Magazine in late 2020.”

The Digest

The National Gallery Singapore ‘s chief curator Patrick Flores and assistant chief executive Chris Lee , are leaving the institution in December, coinciding with the departure of its chief executive and director, Eugene Tan . [ The Straits Times ]

Some 600 Nazi-era artifacts , including personal letters from concentration camps, index cards kept by the Gestapo, and others, will go to museums and will no longer be auctioned in Germany, following an international outcry. [ Monopol ]

British Indian art expert Charles Greig has donated 50 18th and 19th-century artworks made in India to the Tate . [ ARTnews ]

Sotheby’s is holding its first auction in Abu Dhabi on December 10, titled Breaking Ground , following Christie’s first fine art auction in the city on November 1, located at the new Saadiyat Grove Experience Centre on Saadiyat Island. [ The National ]

Archaeologists have discovered a rare shipwreck from the 15th century, believed to be the oldest known Swedish warship. [ Le Figaro ]

The Kicker

IN MEMORIAM . Photographer Miguel Bergasa , who photographed Paraguay’s religious Mennonite community, has died, reports El País . Born in Pamplona, Spain, in 1951, Bergasa was known for his black-and-white documentary photographs of rural festivals and rituals at risk of erasure. “I like to capture images of things you know time will erase. There’s a sense of longing,” he once said.

title_original: [Open Call] Roots & Worlds 2025: Elsewhere, Within
editorial_title_zh: [公开征集] 2025年“根源与世界”：别处，内在

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“根源与世界”（Roots & Worlds）是一个将理论与实践相结合、为期三个月的密集型另类摄影学校。通过公开征集，将选出六位越南新锐摄影师参与，每人将获得6,000,000 VND的制作费及用于发展项目的艺术支持。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025年项目题为《别处，内在》（Elsewhere, Within），由尤金妮·辛克尔（Eugénie Shinkle，英国威斯敏斯特大学）与河桃（Hà Đào）和林范（Linh Phạm，越南Matca）共同领导。申请截止日期为2025年8月31日（含当天）。", "translated": "2025年“根源与世界”（Roots & Worlds 2025）项目获得了英国文化协会“文化连结”资助。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "*本标题借鉴了伊丽莎白·波维内利（Elizabeth Povinelli）的《路线/世界》（Routes/Worlds，2022）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一个信息与机会似乎自由流动、全球公开征集和在线平台承诺实现平等获取的时代，摄影的现实状况依然参差不齐。为了弥合这些差距，“根源与世界”提供了一个结构，支持越南新锐从业者打磨他们的声音并定位其摄影实践，将其作为一种观察世界并理解自身在其中位置的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "标题《别处，内在》（Elsewhere, Within）并非旨在规定参与者的作品内容，而是为了鼓励人们意识到摄影在当今社会、文化和政治气候中不断变化的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如《全球摄影劳特利奇指南》（The Routledge Companion to Global Photographies）所指出：“围绕摄影的生态与去殖民话语揭示了该媒介的全球纠葛：地球一端产生的影像是一度横跨整个地表的劳动的产物。与此同时，对照片的多种方法和理解表明，尽管它看起来可能像是一种通用语言，但我们利用其工具的目的却有着天壤之别。”与其说是从所谓的摄影制作中心向外围灌输知识，“根源与世界”则是以一种探究的精神成型的，它为关于意图和意义的持续反思保留了空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/rootsworlds_2025_web_004-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Matca", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目旨在寻找六位希望发展视觉语言并创作具有社会意识故事的越南职业生涯早期影像创作者。我们强烈鼓励河内和胡志明市以外地区、以及创作和展示作品机会有限的申请者报名。年龄、教育背景和专业经验均不受限制，但具备基本的英语交流能力是先决条件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "是一位以河内为基地的摄影和动态影像艺术家。她的创作灵感源自日常生活中安静的戏剧性，探讨个人命运如何与更宏大的历史相交织，并思考距离的概念，将相机视作见证者与中介。她曾获得多项资助与奖项，包括克劳斯亲王基金会（Prince Claus Fund）的种子奖（Seed Award）、第38届东川赏（Higashikawa Award）以及多格玛奖（Dogma Prize）。", "是一位常驻越南河内的越南摄影师。他的工作聚焦于湄公河下游地区未被充分关注的社群经历，审视气候危机、社会转型、经济快速增长以及地盘政治紧张局势所带来的常被忽视的影响。凭借其现代艺术与设计的背景，Linh 采用了刻意的视觉策略来探讨这些关键议题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两人曾共同设计并领导多个教育项目，包括 Roots & Worlds (2023)、与 NOOR 合作的“视觉化气候危机”（Visualising Climate Crisis with NOOR，2023）以及与皇家墨尔本理工大学（RMIT University）合作的“未来祖先”（Future Ancestors，2023）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "EUGÉNIE SHINKLE 🇬🇧", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eugénie Shinkle 是一位摄影师兼写作者，其作品探讨摄影的感官、物质和政治维度。拥有土木工程背景的她，带来了融合了艺术史、哲学、风景研究和时尚理论的跨学科方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eugénie 的摄影实践以扩展和实验性的方式切入风景，探索时间性、抽象性和非人类能动性等主题。她的作品曾在国际上广泛展出和发表。她是摄影书评论平台 C4 Journal 的编辑，也是摄影界新兴声音的坚定倡导者。Eugénie 尤为热衷于支持那些采用非常规工艺、叙事实验，并对物质性、身份和空间进行批判性介入的摄影师。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/rootsworlds_2025_web_005-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Matca", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "个人陈述中应该包含什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "请向我们介绍你的背景、当前的摄影实践以及感兴趣的领域。是什么促使你从事摄影？请介绍你希望在项目期间探索的作品；这可以是一个全新的项目，也可以是正在进行中的系列作品。我们也欢迎你分享你曾使用过或想要尝试的任何视觉方法。请随时附上你自己的图片或参考资料。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "请注意，由于你的想法和作品在未来几个月中预计会发生显著演变，因此个人陈述应侧重于阐明你的关切、动机和好奇心所在，而不是描述一个最终结果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "选拔标准是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "选拔基于你的作品集的实力与相关性 (50%) 以及你的个人陈述 (50%)。我们欢迎开放、有动力且渴望在摄影之旅中成长的实践者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的作品集应该是什么样的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "请提交一份包含多个项目的单一 PDF 文件，每个项目包含 8-20 张图片，以最好地展现你的兴趣和视觉风格。你也可以包含进行中的作品或单张图片的精选。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我应该提议一个新项目还是进行中的项目？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两者皆可接受。你可以将该项目作为进一步发展正在进行的工作或尝试新方法的平台。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "会考虑哪些摄影流派？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们支持广泛的摄影方法，从纪实到更具实验性的实践，例如将摆拍影像、档案材料以及文字或声音等其他媒介相结合。探索抽象或物质干预的实践者也欢迎申请。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果加入，需要投入多少时间？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "预计每周需要 2-3 小时用于线上课程，外加拍照、阅读和讨论的时间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的英语不是很好。提供翻译支持吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不提供实时翻译，但我们可以提供越南语摘要。由于英语是主要语言，因此需要具备良好的英语沟通能力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我必须在项目期间完成一个完整的项目吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不需要，但预计你在项目期间会有显著的进展。往届参与者在项目结束后也继续扩展他们的项目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加入需要付费吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目免费。入选参与者将获得 6,000,000 VND 的创作资助。对于居住在河内市以外的人，还将报销在河内停留 4 天的差旅和住宿费用。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我必须全程身处越南吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不需要。你可以从任何地方加入线上阶段。但是，你必须在 2025 年 11 月下旬身处河内以参加编辑和开放工作室活动。全勤是强制要求的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "越南海外侨民摄影师可以申请吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不可以。该项目面向持有越南国籍的人士。", "translated": true}]

Through an open call, six emerging Vietnamese photographers will be selected to participate, receiving a production fee of 6,000,000 VND each and artistic support to develop their projects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The inaugural edition in 2023 was co-developed between IC Visual Lab (UK) and Matca (Vietnam) as a mentorship where collaboration takes centre stage. In response to the limited educational and professional opportunities in Vietnam’s photography scene, we set out to create a space where participants can engage with important ideas and approaches in contemporary photography, while participating in hands-on exercises from conceptualization to production, editing, and presentation. It mentored six participants with projects on the theme of Ecological Encounters, and was met with high demand for continuation after the resulting works were showcased in Hanoi, HCMC, and Bristol."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The 2025 edition, titled Elsewhere, Within , is co-led by Eugénie Shinkle (University of Westminster, UK) alongside Hà Đào and Linh Phạm (Matca, Vietnam). The deadline for application submission is Aug 31, 2025(inclusive)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Running from September to November 2025, the program will take place both online and in person. It begins with a series of online lectures, group discussions, and individual tutorials, followed by a 4-day open studio in Hanoi where everyone will gather to collectively edit and present the works to the public."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Roots & Worlds 2025 is supported by the British Council’s Connections Through Culture Grant."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "*The title owes a debt of gratitude to Elizabeth Povinelli’s Routes/Worlds (2022)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In an age where information and opportunities appear to flow freely, where global open calls and online platforms promise equal access, the realities of photography remain uneven. Aiming to address such gaps, Roots & Worlds offers a structure to support emerging Vietnamese practitioners in refining their voices and situating their photographic practice, as both a way of seeing the world and making sense of their place within it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The title Elsewhere, Within is not meant to dictate the content of participants’ works, but to encourage an awareness of photography’s shifting role within today’s social, cultural, and political climate."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As noted in The Routledge Companion to Global Photographies , “Ecological and decolonial discourses around photography reveal the medium’s global entanglements: images produced on one side of the globe are the result of labors which span its full surface. At the same time, the multiplicity of approaches and understandings of the photograph reveal that, even though it might seem like a universal language, we utilize its tools to radically different ends.” Rather than imparting knowledge from a so-called centre of photographic production to the periphery, Roots & Worlds takes shape in a spirit of inquiry, one that holds space for ongoing reflection on intention and meaning."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/rootsworlds_2025_web_004-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Matca"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This program is intended for six early-career Vietnamese image-makers who wish to develop their visual language and produce socially conscious stories. We highly encourage applicants from outside Hanoi and HCMC, and those who have had limited opportunity to make and show works. There are no restrictions on age, educational background and professional experience, but basic communication skills in English are a prerequisite."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The application should include a portfolio, CV, and a statement of no more than 500 words outlining your photographic practice, motivation for applying, and a project or topic you wish to develop within the framework of the program. While all topics and photographic approaches are welcome, priority will be given to proposals that are both feasible and closely aligned with the applicant’s goals. Chosen participants are expected to actively contribute to the sessions and be committed to making work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Please refer to the FAQs below and contact us at hello@matca.vn if you have any other questions about the application process."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Free of charge 3-month program, artistic support throughout the program period, and access to learning materials"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Production fee of 6,000,000 VND per participant"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Travel and accommodation expenses to Hanoi for the 4-day Editing & Open Studio"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Resulting works will be showcased at Matca Space for Photography and online"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Professional network development in Vietnam and the UK"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aug 4"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Launching of the project website and open call"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aug 31"}, while gradually developing their own projects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nov 20-23"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Phase 02 – Open Studio in Hanoi The whole group will gather at Matca Space for Photography to collectively edit and present their works for a public Open Studio event."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "HA DAO 🇻🇳"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "is an artist working with photography and moving image based in Hanoi. Inspired by the quiet drama of everyday life, her work explores how personal fates intersect with larger histories and reflects on the notion of distance, with the camera as both witness and intermediary. She is the recipient of several grants and awards, including the Seed Award by the Prince Claus Fund, the 38th Higashikawa Award, and the Dogma Prize."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "LINH PHAM 🇻🇳"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "is a Vietnamese photographer based in Hanoi, Vietnam. His work focuses on the experiences of underrecognized communities in the Lower Mekong region, examining the often overlooked impacts of climate crises, social transformations, rapid economic growth, and geopolitical tensions. Informed by his background in modern art and design, Linh employs deliberate visual strategies to explore these critical issues."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Both of them have co-designed and led multiple educational initiatives, including Roots & Worlds (2023), Visualising Climate Crisis with NOOR (2023), and Future Ancestors with RMIT University (2023)."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "EUGÉNIE SHINKLE 🇬🇧"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eugénie Shinkle is a photographer and writer whose work explores the sensory, material, and political dimensions of photography. With a background in civil engineering, she brings an interdisciplinary approach that draws on art history, philosophy, landscape studies, and fashion theory."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eugénie’s photographic practice engages with landscape in expanded and experimental terms, exploring themes of temporality, abstraction, and nonhuman agency. It has been widely exhibited and published internationally. She is the editor of C4 Journal, a platform for critical writing on the photobook, and a committed advocate for emerging voices in photography. Eugénie is particularly interested in supporting photographers working with unconventional processes, narrative experimentation, and critical engagement with materiality, identity, and space."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://matca.vn/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/rootsworlds_2025_web_005-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Matca"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What should I include in the statement?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Please tell us about your background, current photographic practice, and areas of interest. article_text:
AN ALTERNATIVE PHOTOGRAPHY SCHOOL THAT COMBINES THEORY AND PRACTICE IN AN INTENSIVE THREE-MONTH PROGRAM

Free program running from September to November 2025

Take place both online and in person in Hanoi

Six selected photographers will receive a production fee of 6,000,000 VND each and artistic support to develop their projects

THE PROGRAM IS SUPPORTED BY THE BRITISH COUNCIL’S CONNECTIONS THROUGH CULTURE GRANT

Roots & Worlds is an alternative photography school that combines theory and practice in an intensive three-month program. Through an open call, six emerging Vietnamese photographers will be selected to participate, receiving a production fee of 6,000,000 VND each and artistic support to develop their projects.

The inaugural edition in 2023 was co-developed between IC Visual Lab (UK) and Matca (Vietnam) as a mentorship where collaboration takes centre stage. In response to the limited educational and professional opportunities in Vietnam’s photography scene, we set out to create a space where participants can engage with important ideas and approaches in contemporary photography, while participating in hands-on exercises from conceptualization to production, editing, and presentation. It mentored six participants with projects on the theme of Ecological Encounters, and was met with high demand for continuation after the resulting works were showcased in Hanoi, HCMC, and Bristol.

The 2025 edition, titled Elsewhere, Within , is co-led by Eugénie Shinkle (University of Westminster, UK) alongside Hà Đào and Linh Phạm (Matca, Vietnam). The deadline for application submission is Aug 31, 2025(inclusive).

Running from September to November 2025, the program will take place both online and in person. It begins with a series of online lectures, group discussions, and individual tutorials, followed by a 4-day open studio in Hanoi where everyone will gather to collectively edit and present the works to the public.

Roots & Worlds 2025 is supported by the British Council’s Connections Through Culture Grant.

*The title owes a debt of gratitude to Elizabeth Povinelli’s Routes/Worlds (2022).

In an age where information and opportunities appear to flow freely, where global open calls and online platforms promise equal access, the realities of photography remain uneven. Aiming to address such gaps, Roots & Worlds offers a structure to support emerging Vietnamese practitioners in refining their voices and situating their photographic practice, as both a way of seeing the world and making sense of their place within it.

The title Elsewhere, Within is not meant to dictate the content of participants’ works, but to encourage an awareness of photography’s shifting role within today’s social, cultural, and political climate.

As noted in The Routledge Companion to Global Photographies , “Ecological and decolonial discourses around photography reveal the medium’s global entanglements: images produced on one side of the globe are the result of labors which span its full surface. At the same time, the multiplicity of approaches and understandings of the photograph reveal that, even though it might seem like a universal language, we utilize its tools to radically different ends.” Rather than imparting knowledge from a so-called centre of photographic production to the periphery, Roots & Worlds takes shape in a spirit of inquiry, one that holds space for ongoing reflection on intention and meaning.

This program is intended for six early-career Vietnamese image-makers who wish to develop their visual language and produce socially conscious stories. We highly encourage applicants from outside Hanoi and HCMC, and those who have had limited opportunity to make and show works. There are no restrictions on age, educational background and professional experience, but basic communication skills in English are a prerequisite.

The application should include a portfolio, CV, and a statement of no more than 500 words outlining your photographic practice, motivation for applying, and a project or topic you wish to develop within the framework of the program. While all topics and photographic approaches are welcome, priority will be given to proposals that are both feasible and closely aligned with the applicant’s goals. Chosen participants are expected to actively contribute to the sessions and be committed to making work.

Please refer to the FAQs below and contact us at hello@matca.vn if you have any other questions about the application process.

Free of charge 3-month program, artistic support throughout the program period, and access to learning materials

Production fee of 6,000,000 VND per participant

Travel and accommodation expenses to Hanoi for the 4-day Editing & Open Studio

Resulting works will be showcased at Matca Space for Photography and online

Professional network development in Vietnam and the UK

Aug 4

Launching of the project website and open call

Aug 31

Application deadline

Sep 7

Announcement of participants

Sep-Nov

Phase 01 – Online lectures, group discussions, and individual tutorials Key topics in contemporary photography will be covered, including: • Research for Practice • Expanded Documentary photography • Feeling, Thinking and Meaning: How Photographs Move Us • Situated Photography Weekly exercises will encourage participants to experiment with various approaches while gradually developing their own projects.

Nov 20-23

Phase 02 – Open Studio in Hanoi The whole group will gather at Matca Space for Photography to collectively edit and present their works for a public Open Studio event.

HA DAO 🇻🇳

is an artist working with photography and moving image based in Hanoi. Inspired by the quiet drama of everyday life, her work explores how personal fates intersect with larger histories and reflects on the notion of distance, with the camera as both witness and intermediary. She is the recipient of several grants and awards, including the Seed Award by the Prince Claus Fund, the 38th Higashikawa Award, and the Dogma Prize.

LINH PHAM 🇻🇳

is a Vietnamese photographer based in Hanoi, Vietnam. His work focuses on the experiences of underrecognized communities in the Lower Mekong region, examining the often overlooked impacts of climate crises, social transformations, rapid economic growth, and geopolitical tensions. Informed by his background in modern art and design, Linh employs deliberate visual strategies to explore these critical issues.

Both of them have co-designed and led multiple educational initiatives, including Roots & Worlds (2023), Visualising Climate Crisis with NOOR (2023), and Future Ancestors with RMIT University (2023).

EUGÉNIE SHINKLE 🇬🇧

Eugénie Shinkle is a photographer and writer whose work explores the sensory, material, and political dimensions of photography. With a background in civil engineering, she brings an interdisciplinary approach that draws on art history, philosophy, landscape studies, and fashion theory.

Eugénie’s photographic practice engages with landscape in expanded and experimental terms, exploring themes of temporality, abstraction, and nonhuman agency. It has been widely exhibited and published internationally. She is the editor of C4 Journal, a platform for critical writing on the photobook, and a committed advocate for emerging voices in photography. Eugénie is particularly interested in supporting photographers working with unconventional processes, narrative experimentation, and critical engagement with materiality, identity, and space.

What should I include in the statement?

Please tell us about your background, current photographic practice, and areas of interest. What motivates you to pursue photography? Introduce the project you’d like to explore during the program; this can be either a new or an ongoing body of work. You’re also welcome to share any visual approaches you’ve used or want to experiment with. Feel free to include your own images or reference material.

Please note that since your ideas and work are expected to evolve significantly over the upcoming months, the statement should focus on articulating your concerns, motivations, and areas of curiosity, rather than describing an outcome.

What are the selection criteria?

Selection is based on the strength and relevance of your portfolio (50%) and your statement (50%). We welcome practitioners who are open, motivated, and eager to grow in their photography journeys.

What should my portfolio look like?

Submit a single PDF showcasing several projects, each with 8-20 images, that best represent your interests and visual style. You may also include work-in-progress or a selection of single images.

Should I propose a new or ongoing project?

Both are accepted. You can use the program as a platform to further develop an ongoing work or experiment with new approaches.

What genre of photography is considered?

We accommodate a wide range of photographic approaches, from documentary to more experimental practices, for example, combining staged imagery, archival material, and other media such as text or sound. Practitioners exploring abstraction or material interventions are also welcome to apply.

What is the time commitment if I join?

Expect 2-3 hours/week for online sessions, plus time for photographing, reading, and discussions.

My English is not very good. Is translation support available?

There is no live translation, but we can provide summaries in Vietnamese. A good command of English is required as it is the main language.

Do I need to complete a full project within the program?

No, but you are expected to make significant progress within the program duration. Participants in the past edition have also continued to expand on their projects after the program concluded.

Are there any fees to join?

The program is free of charge. Selected participants will receive a 6,000,000 VND production grant. Travel and accommodation for 4 days in Hanoi are also covered for those based outside of the city.

Do I have to be based in Vietnam the whole time?

No. You can join the online phase from anywhere. However, you must be in Hanoi in late November 2025 to join the editing and open studio. Full attendance is mandatory.

Can photographers from the Vietnamese diaspora apply?

No. The program is for those with Vietnamese citizenship.
