article_text:
«Abbiamo tempo». Ce lo diciamo per rimandare una decisione, per rassicurarci, per allontanare il pensiero di ciò che potrebbe finire. Lo ripetono anche i protagonisti di Coro degli amanti , quasi fosse una formula capace di tenere a distanza l’imprevisto, la malattia, la perdita. E intanto il tempo passa, si accumula nei gesti, nelle abitudini, nelle parole dette mille volte, fino a confondere due esistenze in una sola. È dentro questa contraddizione, tra l’illusione di avere tutto il tempo davanti e la sua inevitabile finitezza, che si muove il testo scritto da Tiago Rodrigues nel 2006, oggi in scena al Piccolo Teatro Grassi di Milano , nella sua prima regia in lingua italiana, con Isabella Ragonese e Francesco Alberici .

Si comincia con un’emergenza. Una coppia sta guardando Scarface sul divano quando lei viene colpita da un attacco d’asma. La corsa disperata verso l’ospedale, il timore di non arrivare in tempo, la paura della morte. Poi il pericolo passa e la vita riprende, con la rassicurante convinzione di avere ancora tempo. Da quel momento il racconto attraversa un’esistenza condivisa, tra lavoro, figli, piccoli conflitti domestici e progetti rimandati.

La particolarità della scrittura sta nella sua costruzione polifonica. I protagonisti parlano spesso all’unisono, in una partitura serrata in cui le voci si sovrappongono, si inseguono e talvolta si contraddicono. Lui pronuncia i pensieri di lei, lei quelli di lui, come se il tempo trascorso insieme avesse progressivamente reso indistinguibili memorie e identità. Ragonese e Alberici abitano con precisione questo meccanismo, restituendo naturalezza a una struttura tutt’altro che semplice.

Anche lo spazio scenico procede per sottrazione. Una superficie simile a terriccio, due sedie che diventano di volta in volta divano, letto d’ospedale o sala d’attesa, una piccola console con un bollitore per il tè e un tavolino con un giradischi. Pochi elementi mobili, sufficienti a evocare gli ambienti di una vita.

C’è qualcosa di profondamente riconoscibile nelle esistenze che attraversano Coro degli amanti . Sono vite ordinarie, borghesi, fatte di sentimenti, abitudini, piccole fratture e parole che sembrano appartenere anche a noi. Un film guardato sul divano, una figlia che diventa vegetariana, le discussioni familiari: dettagli che suscitano le risate del pubblico, chiamato a ritrovare sulla scena frammenti della propria quotidianità.

È una prossimità che Rodrigues coltiva con delicatezza, affidando alle piccole cose il compito di raccontare le grandi questioni dell’esistenza: l’amore, il tempo, la malattia, la morte. Eppure, nel susseguirsi di situazioni così familiari, il racconto sembra talvolta trovare proprio nella loro riconoscibilità il proprio punto d’arrivo. La vita scorre, si lascia osservare, commuove o diverte, senza che le sue contraddizioni vengano necessariamente portate altrove.

Rimane allora soprattutto la qualità di un duetto, la precisione degli interpreti, l’intuizione di due voci che finiscono per diventare una sola. E quel continuo «abbiamo tempo», che risuona come una promessa e insieme come un’illusione. Forse la più comune, e la più umana, di tutte.

article_text:
The 45th Vancouver International Film Festival ( VIFF ) featured some high-profile titles, including Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” which has been generating awards buzz for star Julianne Moore, and Martin McDonagh’s closing-night black comedy “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky” took home the Audience Award in the Special Presentations category.

Yet beyond the marquee titles, VIFF’s lineup spanned 76 countries and offered plenty of discoveries from established auteurs and emerging filmmakers alike. From Matthew Rankin’s experimental take on Brian Mulroney to Tizza Covi’s portrait of an aging blues musician facing eviction, these eight narrative and documentary films approached familiar subjects from unexpected angles or offered a glimpse into lives rarely captured on film.

Related Stories

Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’

“The Loneliest Man in Town” (Tizza Covi and Rainer Frimmel, Be For Films, Austria, Panorama)

Popular on Variety

A melancholy and deeply nostalgic portrait of an aging Vienna-based blues musician who is the only holdout tenant of an about-to-be-demolished apartment building where he had spent his entire life. As he says goodbye to his home and possessions — which include vintage blues records, memorabilia and an out-of-tune piano — he ponders the prospects of a new beginning elsewhere, even as he’s firmly in the last chapter of his life.

“Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney” (Matthew Rankin, NFB, Canada, Showcase)

Probably one of the most psychedelic and unconventional historical documentaries in recent memory. Rankin forgoes talking heads entirely, instead remixing archival footage, animation, and music to trace Mulroney’s rise to power in what feels like an experimental vintage fever dream. Rather than examine the late Canadian prime minister’s political impact and legacy, the film explores how his image was built and how his party transformed along the way.

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” (Noah Segan, Sony Pictures Classics, U.S., Special Presentations)

John Turturro plays an aging pickpocket whose old-school craft is becoming obsolete in a cashless world. After targeting the wrong mark, he finds himself entangled in a dangerous situation with a crime family and is forced to race against a clock to save his disabled wife. Segan uses the crime thriller genre to tell a deeper story about the nature of progress and how the world moves on, leaving certain people behind along with the shared values, ways of life and technologies they once trusted. With its melancholy jazz score, it’s an elegy to a New York that’s slipping away.

“School for Defectors” (Jeremy Workman, South Korea, U.S., Showcase)

This hopeful documentary follows teenagers attending Jangdaehyun School in Busan, which helps the children of North Korean defectors to navigate life in South Korea. As they struggle to adjust, many deal with insecurity, shame, trauma and discrimination. The school works to give them confidence, purpose, meaning and a sense of belonging, while also helping them understand what their parents fled. For a number of students, the full story of their family’s escape is revealed for the first time on camera.

“Minotaur” ( Andrey Zvyagintsev , Mubi, France, Germany, Latvia, Special Presentations)

Zvyagintsev meticulously constructs a window into the life of Gleb, the CEO of a Russian transport company who occupies a sleek modern home with his wife and son, but there’s a clear disconnect between them. When Gleb discovers his wife’s infidelity, it sends him on a particularly dark path, with moments of morbid humor intertwined. In the background, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is on-going, and the military is scrambling for recruits. The town’s mayor pressures Gleb and other executives to hand over employees for the draft. His household becomes a microcosm of a broader societal moral decay, fuelled by detachment, indifference, corruption, complacency and the pursuit of comfort. A Cannes Festival Grand Prix winner.

“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” ( William Greaves, David Greaves, Neon, U.S., Insights)

Imagine being a fly on the wall at a dinner party attended by some of the most influential figures in Black cultural life. In 1972, filmmaker William Greaves gathered artists and intellectuals associated with the Harlem Renaissance for an intimate dinner party at Duke Ellington’s home, capturing their conversations on 16mm. Now completed by his son, David Greaves, this documentary offers an intimate time capsule of a generation’s wit, debates and unmistakable style — inviting audiences to spend an evening in the company of history.

“The Flight” (Soran Mardookhi, NFB, Canada, Showcase)

The downing of Ukraine International Airlines Flight PS752 in January 2020 killed all 176 people aboard, many of them Iranian Canadians. The incident devastated the families of the victims and shook the Iranian diaspora. Mardookhi follows three grieving Iranian-Canadian families who seeking answers and accountability from the Islamic Republic of Iran years after tragedy. Through stories the victims become more than just names in a news report or a statistic, but rather individuals whose absence continues to affect those left behind.

“Diary of a Chambermaid” ( Radu Jude , Ritual Films, France, Romania, Showcase)

Jude’s modern twist on Octave Mirbeau’s novel follows Gianina (Ana Dumitrașcu), a Romanian migrant working as a live-in housekeeper and nanny for a wealthy family in present-day Bordeaux. Her young daughter waits at home in Romania, growing more upset with each video call and each postponed promise of a return. At her employers’ recommendation, Gianina also joins an amateur stage production of “The Diary of a Chambermaid,” with scenes from its rehearsals interspersed throughout the film. The film is built on juxtapositions: the care she gives her employers’ son versus the FaceTime sessions she can offer her own daughter. An elegant French home against rural Romania. The performative progressive speeches by her employers in contrast to how Gianina is actually viewed. And her outwardly warm, accommodating demeanour while the thoughts she shares with her mother or mutters under her breath are rather different.

article_text:
Bleecker Street , the indie distribution label behind the U.S. releases of Alex Gibney’s documentary “Musk,” Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care,” Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation,” along with last year’s “Spinal Tap II: The End Continues,” “Rebuilding,” and “Bone Lake,” and many more titles, has been acquired by Outerlight Entertainment, formerly known as First Look.

The acquisition comes after the distributor’s founder and then-CEO, Andrew Karpen, died from an aggressive form of brain cancer at the age of 59 in May 2025.

The Bleecker Street brand joins Outerlight’s Topic Studios , but the two labels will continue to operate separately. Among Outerlight’s portfolio, the company also owns Puzzle Pictures, with investments in MHz Choice and Passionflix.

Bleecker Street CEO Kent Sanderson and its president and chief marketing officer Tyler DiNapoli will remain with the banner. The release announcing the deal also states that Bleecker will retain control of its current slate without disruption, along with its other acquisitions, filmmaker relationships, and marketing and distribution operations.

“Bleecker Street is growing, and our ambition is to continue scaling the company while staying true to what has always made us distinctive,” said Sanderson in a statement. “Outerlight shares our belief in the power of cinema and the importance of theatrical moviegoing, and its long-term backing gives us additional capacity to pursue the opportunities we see across our core film business as well as compelling new avenues in the film space. We’re excited about what we can build from here.”

Financial details of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Earlier this year, Bleecker Street notched the record for the highest-grossing live theater capture ever with its release of “Hadestown: The Musical” through its event label Crosswalk. The film earned more than $20 million during a limited theatrical run, becoming one of the sleeper hits of the summer box office.

Karpen founded the New York-based Bleecker Street in 2014. Prior to creating the banner, he had been serving as co-CEO of Focus Features since 2006; he elected to leave the company in 2013 as restructuring by Universal would’ve forced him to relocate his family to Los Angeles. Bleeker counts “Logan Lucky,” “Leave No Trace,” “Captain Fantastic” and “Trumbo” among its most notable releases.
excerpt_original: CEO Kent Sanderson will continue to lead the indie distribution label independently.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "M ore than a flowering of the arts at the dawn of the 20th century, the Harlem Renaissance marked the breakthrough moment when Black Americans asserted their creative control, defining a culture that had been purpose-built to exclude them. The imprints were all over the Jazz Age – on bookshelves and radio, in flapper dresses and cloche hats, in Hubert Julian’s daring flights and the fractious debates between Marcus Garvey and WEB Du Bois."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Like the David committee of the Italian Renaissance or the American Revolution’s Continental Congress, the Harlem Renaissance is one of those moments that makes you wonder: what was it really like? The Dark Tower salons? Those Cotton Club nights? The rent parties with all those New Negroes – a heady brew of southern émigrés, Caribbean vanguards and New York lifers – holding forth and hootin’ and hollerin’, high on the fact that they had found one another? Could they appreciate the significance of the moment as they were making it? “I remember being in Brooklyn in the 1990s and seeing various artists around,” says film-maker Liani Greaves, reflecting on her early career working with Tupac on Above the Rim and the director Hype Williams on Biggie music videos. “Brooklyn Moon Cafe was the spot. Sometimes we forget that it is The Now. We’re constantly looking to the next thing, looking outside.”", "links": [{"text": "David committee", "url": "https://www.britannica.com/today-in-history/September-8-1504-Michelangelos-David-Unveiled"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Once Upon a Time in Harlem looks back – to the August day in 1972 when Liani’s grandfather, the prolific and pioneering film-maker William Greaves, threw a cocktail party at Duke Ellington House, invited over the surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance and switched on the cameras. article_text:
M ore than a flowering of the arts at the dawn of the 20th century, the Harlem Renaissance marked the breakthrough moment when Black Americans asserted their creative control, defining a culture that had been purpose-built to exclude them. The imprints were all over the Jazz Age – on bookshelves and radio, in flapper dresses and cloche hats, in Hubert Julian’s daring flights and the fractious debates between Marcus Garvey and WEB Du Bois.

Like the David committee of the Italian Renaissance or the American Revolution’s Continental Congress, the Harlem Renaissance is one of those moments that makes you wonder: what was it really like? The Dark Tower salons? Those Cotton Club nights? The rent parties with all those New Negroes – a heady brew of southern émigrés, Caribbean vanguards and New York lifers – holding forth and hootin’ and hollerin’, high on the fact that they had found one another? Could they appreciate the significance of the moment as they were making it? “I remember being in Brooklyn in the 1990s and seeing various artists around,” says film-maker Liani Greaves, reflecting on her early career working with Tupac on Above the Rim and the director Hype Williams on Biggie music videos. “Brooklyn Moon Cafe was the spot. Sometimes we forget that it is The Now. We’re constantly looking to the next thing, looking outside.”

Once Upon a Time in Harlem looks back – to the August day in 1972 when Liani’s grandfather, the prolific and pioneering film-maker William Greaves, threw a cocktail party at Duke Ellington House, invited over the surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance and switched on the cameras. (With Ellington himself too ill to attend, it fell to his sister, Ruth, to play host.) For four hours, these extraordinary partygoers – some seeing one another for the first time in 50 years – reminisced, made merry and reckoned with the Harlem Renaissance’s modern-day legacy. The 100-minute film itself is a time capsule, a cinematic Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in which the Harlem Renaissance gazes back at its own legacy, leaving future generations to unearth, interrogate and work from the reflections they find.

It’s the kind of artefact today’s Black creatives should have in their library – for inspiration, for accountability, to ground themselves. But until hard copies are available – “That will exist!” says William’s son, director David Greaves, adding that streaming is still a long way off – audiences will have to catch Once Upon a Time in theaters, as the film opens nationwide this month. “We’ve always imagined people coming in groups, going with their family,” says Liani, a producer on the film. “We want people to be in community, visit with the film, and really experience it in that way.”

Following in the tradition of A Great Day in Harlem, the documentary about Art Kane’s stunning photograph of jazz greats gathered on Harlem stoop, Once Upon a Time is a home movie in every sense. William Greaves – an Actors Studio member alongside Marlon Brando before directing the groundbreaking meta-documentary Symbiopsychotaxiplasm – devoted himself to the project until his death in 2014 at age 87. Greaves kept rolling after the party, through the 80s and 90s. Liani remembers William and his wife, Louise Archambault Greaves, turning up with their cameras to a Harlem Aids walk she was working in the 2000s. Among Liani and David’s inheritances was some 60,000 feet of 16mm film held in storage. “I think they were shooting a lot of events, looking for evidence of the Harlem Renaissance,” Liani says. “But it felt to me that they had kind of lost their way. And just like in Symbiopsychotaxiplasm, he had to kind of step away in order for the film to be great.”

So Liani and David kept the focus squarely on the party. They enlisted the help of preservation specialist Bill Brand to restore the 1972 footage, an 18-month process, before sending it off to a finishing house. “They did stuff that we could never have done 50 years ago,” David says. “Color correction, cleaning and also – I’ll be honest – taking hair out of the gate.” The results are visible in the richness, warmth and texture of the footage – the kind of craftsmanship movie-making used to be about.

And then the titans of the Harlem Renaissance start filling the frame: the photographer James Van Der Zee, demurring from an invitation to play Duke’s piano before letting his shockingly nimble fingers wander. Ragtime composer Eubie Blake reeling back to the time the papers misquoted him saying he’d never extend his hand to a white man. (He said he’d never extend it first , a distinction that mattered under segregation.) Regina Andrews, the essential librarian and curator, considered whether a Black artist could have worked in isolation while the movement was happening around them. “There was no way not to be caught up,” she says. “You were pulled along.”

As the 1972 reunion unfolds, the film scrambles to capture every moment, following the connections and conversations across three rooms. David was part of the six-man crew his father assembled for the shoot, each member having to split their attention between the scene unfolding before them and whatever might be bubbling up somewhere else. There’s a lovely moment when one cameraman catches William slating him on from the edge of a scene, the silent soundman confirming with his eyes as another cameraman crosses the shot. (Syncing the picture to the sound was another puzzle that came together in restoration.)

As William strains to impose a bit of film-making order on action already beyond his control, it’s clear he wouldn’t have it any other way, that he’s getting exactly what he wants from this crowd – big personalities, lively crosstalk, a tangible sense of those bygone salons. Partygoers in their 70s and 80s, flashing their modern finery, are stirred to youthful passion when the subjects that once animated them resurface – especially in the one-on-one interviews William Greaves shot with some Renaissance contributors after the party. “My father had them wear the same clothes so they would not be clashing,” David remembers fondly.

It’s hard not to be awestruck when the Negro Actors Guild president, Leigh Whipper, drops into his Haile Selassie monologue from the Stalinist film Mission to Moscow, or when the civil rights activist Richard B Moore delivers a perfect recitation of the Claude McKay’s poem If We Must Die on cue. “I always say this is what it looks like when your brain is not on electronics,” Liani says. “I have to imagine many of them were writing with one another, to one another – some by hand, which is a different kind of brain skill. They were brilliant people.”

The Harlem romantics also had a knack for expressing their disagreements with one another in erudite style – polite shade, we call it now. In one meaty scene, the multimedia artist Romare Bearden takes exception to the way artists like him were minimized in the seminal book on the Harlem Renaissance by Nathan Huggins; the Harvard professor is standing across the room, holding it. Huggins, though, does offer a credible defense – arguing that art and music are intrinsically more difficult to translate than the written word. “It is kind of poetic, the way they clap back,” Liani says. “It’s all in love and friendship.”

Still, there wasn’t genuine affection for everyone in the room. Apparently, the presence of George Schuyler – the commentator who came up during the Renaissance before turning against progressivism and, later, the civil rights movement – was met with twisted faces and cold shoulders. One barb directed at him was cut out entirely. It speaks to the depth of the disagreements among the Renaissance’s vanguards, and the intensity with which they still cared. “It’s like [Garveyite community organizer] Thomas Harvey said at the end of the film: ‘We were on different roads, but all going toward the same goal,’” David says. “It shows that the Renaissance was not a monolith of thinking.”

But the issue that really hung over the party was how the Harlem Renaissance would be remembered. Already, William’s guests were lamenting how the younger generation had moved on to zeitgeistier fare: comic books, funk music, blaxploitation films. David Greaves makes a point of tracking the change his father set out to chronicle in the documentary, moving from James Van Der Zee’s gorgeous black-and-white photographs of the neighborhood in full flower to William’s 70s footage of vacant faces and graffiti-strewn walls.

Now those kids are the ones clamoring for respect for their artistic contributions. It shows how quickly times change, and how much Black creatives stand to gain by looking to the past as they take the culture forward. “I often think about this film as a recipe for a renaissance,” Liani says. “If you watch, the [Black Renaissance vanguards] tell you what to do. They talk about the importance of being in community, of being audacious. That’s how you create a moment.“

Once Upon a Time in Harlem is out in US cinemas now and in the UK and Australia at a later date

article_text:
When it was announced, in 2017, that the Chilean writer-director Sébastian Lelio was to helm a U.S. remake of his 2013 breakout film “ Gloria ,” admirers of the original — and indeed of Lelio himself — had cause for concern. English-language do-overs of world cinema successes frequently go awry; furthermore, we had the cautionary tale of Dutchman George Sluizer, who directed a hopeless 1993 remake of his own impeccable 1988 chiller “The Vanishing,” to remind us that even having the original filmmaker in charge was no guarantee against a travesty.

Related Stories

Man Arrested on ‘Miami Vice ‘85’ Brooklyn Set After Brandishing a Knife

‘I Play Rocky’ Star Stephan James on Paying Tribute to Carl Weathers with His Red Carpet Look: ‘I Can Literally Walk in His Shoes Yet Again’

The news came at a crucial moment in Lelio’s career. The first of his two films to premiere in 2017, the vibrant, heartfelt transgender character study “ A Fantastic Woman ,” was riding a wave of festival and critical success that began with a Best Screenplay win at the Berlinale, and culminated with an Oscar for Best International Feature (or Best Foreign Language Film, as the award was still called then) — the first ever win for a Chilean film in the category, sealing a resurgence of the country’s cinema also being led by such contemporaries as Sebastián Silva and Lelio’s own producer Pablo Larraín.

The second, “ Disobedience ,” was Lelio’s English-language debut — another story of queer identity, but an altogether different tonal and stylistic proposition. A sober portrayal of an illicit romance between two women from North London’s strict Orthodox Jewish community, it was sensitively observed and beautifully acted by leads Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams, with a restraint that was occasionally countered by moments of frank, charged sensuality. The contrast between “A Fantastic Woman” and “Disobedience” confirmed Lelio as a particularly empathetic and versatile teller of women’s stories — and “Gloria,” a warm and unsentimentally joyous comedy of a fiftysomething divorcée’s reawakening, was also good one. But why go back, when his career was barreling forward?

As it turned out, Lelio knew better than his doubters. The remake, which eventually premiered in 2019 as “ Gloria Bell ,” hewed close to the template of the original, largely inheriting its pleasures and poignancies. But if that makes it sound redundant, it proved a canny and fascinating exercise in performer-as-auteur influence: It was clear that Lelio, self-evidently a champion of women on screen, was interested to see how a wholly different actress would change the tone and temperature of his original story.

A lot, we learned. Paulina García was a funny and resilient force of nature in the 2013 original; in “Gloria Bell,” Julianne Moore brought a yearning, lonely fragility to the material that gave even the film’s uplifting trajectory an undertow of melancholy. The remake got less than its due — Moore, at the very least, deserved some awards attention that year — but it sits beside “Gloria” as an illuminating companion piece rather than a competing interpretation.

I lead with the two Glorias because their respective successes improbably prove a truth about Lelio, a restlessly curious and compassionate filmmaker who passed away, far too soon, on Friday, aged just 52: Even when ostensibly making the same film twice, he never made the same film twice.

His 2005 debut “The Sacred Family” was confident and a bit scrappy, its handheld jaggedness far removed from his later polish, its droll comic tale of a bourgeois man falling for his son’s girlfriend also distinct from the searching feminist portraiture that would define his later career. But it was lively and promising, made in a semi-improvised fashion that he carried forward into his next, more complex film, the troubled youth study “Navidad,” which made its way into the 2009 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight program. But his third film, 2011’s “The Year of the Tiger,” was a considerably more sophisticated effort: an exquisitely understated exploration of faith, guilt and trauma in the wake of Chile’s devastating 2010 earthquake.

“The Year of the Tiger,” which competed at Locarno, was too soulful and richly considered a work on its own terms to be seen as a bid for arthouse-major status — but that’s how it worked out anyway, even if the film didn’t get quite the global exposure it deserved. But by the time “Gloria” came along two years later, the word on Lelio was out and expectations were high: The film was selected for the main competition at Berlin and was an immediate, ebulliently received crowdpleaser. If Larraín had established himself as the dark prince of new Chilean cinema with spiky, perverse, politically bristling works like “Post Mortem” and “No,” Lelio was poised to become its great humanist: his touch light but not soft, his perspective probing but not abrasive.

“A Fantastic Woman,” four years later, delivered on that promise. Propelled by trans star Daniela Vega’s extraordinary, emotionally unguarded performance, its story of a grieving trans woman spurned by the prejudiced family of her dead lover arrived at a vital tipping point for the visibility of transgender narratives and artists in popular culture, and delicately essayed an arc of emphatic, even triumphant self-definition amid a climate of isolation and rejection — all without feeling glibly or opportunistically issue-driven. It was to Lelio’s credit that he was fairly self-effacing in his promotion of the film, letting Vega — with whom he had closely developed the protagonist, aligned with her experience — be its chief ambassador and spokesperson.

“A Fantastic Woman” earned Lelio the most acclaim and kudos of his career — though his finest film as a director, to my mind, was comparatively shortchanged. A period drama set in 19th-century Ireland and adapted from a novel by “Room” author Emma Donoghue, “ The Wonder ” didn’t outwardly look or feel much like a Lelio joint — with its austerely repressed milieu shot, by Ari Wegner, with such a damp, chilly verdigris finish you could practically sense moss growing on the screen as you watched. Yet its story of feminine resolve and dueling moral and spiritual convictions meshed well with the director’s interests, as did Florence Pugh’s tenacious, stout-hearted performance; the film’s earthy folktale trappings stood in exciting contrast to its stark formalist construction.

If “The Wonder” was an ambitious and grandly realized reach, I was less sold on the huge stylistic swing of Lelio’s most recent film, last year’s political musical “The Wave,” which returned him to his homeland. Inspired by a national spate of #MeToo-related feminist student protests that shut down universities across Chile in 2018, it was rhetorically heavy-handed but composed and choreographed with dynamic aplomb, positively thrilling to the spectacle of massed bodies in motion: I wrote in my review that it made one eager to see Lelio tackle more musical fare on screen, never thinking that the film would be his last.

In one of “The Wave’s” more playful flourishes, the fourth wall is broken to acknowledge Lelio’s own presence as the director of the movie — and to ask, pointedly, what a male director was doing on this expressly feminist project anyway. It’s a wink-wink joke that more seriously encapsulated the generous, conscientious, community-minded approach that Lelio brought to his filmmaking: His auteur signature was subtly distinctive, yet he never made himself the star of his work.

U-NEXTで 関連作品を見る PR

解説・あらすじ

香港の伝統的イベント「香港国際ドラゴンボートレース」を題材に、逆境を乗り越えようと奮闘する男たちの姿を通して“中年の危機”という社会問題に切り込んだ大人の青春ドラマ。 社内で勃発したリストラ騒動に巻き込まれ、成り行きからボートレースに出場する羽目に陥った4人の中年男性。私生活でもそれぞれ問題を抱え目標を失っていた彼らは、レースを通じて人生に対する情熱を取り戻していく。 出演は「エグザイル 絆」のフランシス・ン、「幻愛 夢の向こうに」のプーン・チャンリョン、後に「トワイライト・ウォリアーズ 決戦！九龍城砦」でも共演するケニー・ウォンとトニー・ウー。「モンスター・ハント 王の末裔」「エンジェル・バトラー 戦闘無双」などの脚本を手がけたサニー・チャンが長編初メガホンをとった。香港では2018年7月に公開されるとSNSや口コミで話題を集め、3カ月超のロングランヒットを記録。第38回香港電影金像奨では最優秀作品賞を含む11部門にノミネートされた。

editorial_title_zh: 档案：让-弗朗索瓦·容维尔，温柔的柔情
editorial_excerpt_zh: 让-弗朗索瓦·容维尔被死神攫走，其突然一如他毕生所拍的那些照片。正如他的一生致力于捕捉这些偷来的瞬间，死亡也如法炮制，在生命正盛时将他带走。一月初发现的肿瘤……

"让-弗朗索瓦·容维尔于1980年代为《Photo》杂志拍摄的第二组作品，专拍法国女演员。这本书收录了弗雷德里克·贝格伯德一篇动人的序言，其后是一篇简短传记：", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让-弗朗索瓦·容维尔被死神攫走，其突然一如他毕生所拍的那些照片。正如他的一生致力于捕捉这些偷来的瞬间，死亡也如法炮制，在生命正盛时将他带走。一月初发现的肿瘤，仅仅两周后便是最后的告别。他转瞬即逝。当我翻着这位友人最后一本书的书页，双眼模糊了。我的泪水把容维尔的照片化开，融成大卫·汉密尔顿式的柔焦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "容维尔的作品常被套用那句由来已久的说法，被形容为“性感而不低俗”。我更喜欢他自己对所求之物的描述：“la poésie du quotidien”，“日常的诗意”。照片凝固真实的瞬间，你要做的只是挑出那些做得最好的。“我告诉自己，现在和未来都不存在，”他也常这样说，“每个人，每一天，都在创造自己的过去。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让他的影像比其余作品更动人的，是其中的脆弱。容维尔教给我一个至关重要的道理：在摄影中，一如在文学中，重要的是感受。情色与柔情并非不共戴天的仇敌。一只覆着绒毛的手臂，一段纤弱的后颈，一只微微翘起的乳房，床单下背部的曲线，湿润的头发，合上的眼睑，颈上的一记吻痕——所有这些都能令人心动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "容维尔镜头下的女人清新自然，因为她们并未意识到我们的注视。容维尔让我们全都成了满怀爱慕的窥视者。他向我们展示异性恋何以能如此痛苦：无处不在，在每一座房子、每一间浴室里，天堂都潜伏着。天堂轻轻脱下她的T恤，刷牙，臀部紧翘，胸部的曲线绷紧，超越时间。忽然，天堂在静默中分开双腿，咬着指甲，直直望进你的眼睛，在床单上等你时挑逗着你。容维尔如今身在天堂，但对他而言一切未曾改变：他在世时便已身在其中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我像往常一样惊叹地凝视这些影像——它们与那些熟悉的陈词滥调相去甚远——我的思绪转向他使之不朽的那些美丽女人。照片固定住稍纵即逝之物，使短暂者不朽。容维尔拍摄过的许多女人如今已年老或已离世，但——多亏这位如今也已离世的摄影师——她们的完美永不褪色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "容维尔的每一张照片都是一份爱的宣言。有一天，应我的请求，他为我女儿的母亲德尔菲娜·瓦莱特拍了照。我想送给我所爱的这位深发女子一幅肖像。我从未感到自己如此像个戴绿帽的人——尽管是以最情色的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "美是一种转瞬即逝的谜，有些艺术家有能力将其捕捉。当我再次凝视这些美妙的影像，我想起那部美国喜剧的片名《Drop Dead Gorgeous》。容维尔的作品整体而言并非一曲女性气质的颂歌；它讲述的故事，是通过对欲望的颂扬来战胜死亡的战斗。所有这些被猝然捕捉的肩头，这些半露的乳房，这些优美拱起的脚背，这些无瑕的背脊，这份感官的孤独，这两场风暴之间的平静，所有这些满不在乎的美丽女人，都不过是一扇扇轻轻推开的门，透过它们，我们得以窥见永恒的生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "弗雷德里克·贝格伯德", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "让-弗朗索瓦·容维尔1943年出生于法国南部的卡瓦永。不久后他将卖掉著名的甜瓜去买哈苏相机。他的灵感来自巴尔蒂斯、培根、席勒的绘画，但真正的影响来自曼凯维奇、刘别谦、弗里茨·朗、奥逊·威尔斯、阿瑟·佩恩、明内利的电影，以及更近的特里·吉列姆——他承认自己把吉列姆的《巴西》看了十一遍；最后是他最偏爱的电影：弗朗索瓦·特吕弗的《朱尔与吉姆》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1959年，摄影师乔治·格拉斯伯格引导他接触摄影，带他走遍法国各地的教堂。那是一次摄影的启示，此后再未离开他。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "20岁时，他成为美国摄影师理查德·阿维顿的助手。在这段充实的经历之后，他成了自己的“大师”，而他最偏爱的拍摄对象将是女人。他的母亲和他一直十分亲近的小妹妹将成为他“第一批心甘情愿的受害者”。随后是第一位“缪斯”兼同谋蒂娜·斯波托拉罗，他于1982年与她相识，并与她拍出了自己一些最美的影像。再之后是贝阿特丽丝、米里亚姆以及许多其他人……", "translated": true}, article_text:
Archives – October 13, 2011

The second portfolio, which Jean-François Jonvelle began for Photo in the 1980s, is devoted to French actresses. The book features a lovely preface by Frédéric Beigbeder, followed by a short biography:

Jean-François Jonvelle was snatched by the hand of death with a suddenness to match the photographs that were his life. Just as that life was dedicated to capturing these stolen moments, so death followed suit, carrying him off in the midst of life. A tumour discovered in early January, a final farewell just a fortnight later. He was gone in a flash. As I turn the pages of my friend’s last book my eyes mist over. My tears dissolve Jonvelle’s photographs into the soft focus of a David Hamilton.

Jonvelle’s work is often described as being – in the time-honoured formula – ‘sexy but not vulgar’. I prefer his own description of what he sought out: ‘la poésie du quotidien’, ‘the poetry of the everyday’. Photographs freeze moments of truth, all you have to do is choose the ones that do it best. ‘I tell myself that the present and the future don’t exist,’ he also used to say. ‘Everyone, every day, creates their own past.’

The quality that makes his images more moving than the rest is their vulnerability. Jonvelle taught me one crucial lesson: in photography, as in literature, what counts is feeling. Eroticism and tenderness are not sworn enemies. A downy arm, the frail nape of a neck, an uptilted breast, the curve of a back beneath the sheets, damp hair, closed eyelids, the trace of a kiss on the neck all these can be arousing.

Jonvelle’s women are fresh and natural because they are unaware of our gaze. Jonvelle makes adoring voyeurs of us all. He shows us why heterosexuality can be so painful: everywhere, in every house and every bathroom, paradise lurks. Paradise delicately removes her T-shirt, brushes her teeth, buttocks pert, the curve of her breasts taut, timeless. Suddenly paradise parts her legs in silence, biting her fin- gernails as she looks you straight in the eye, teasing you as she waits for you on the sheets. Jonvelle is in paradise now, but for him nothing has changed: he was already there in his lifetime.

As I gaze in wonder, the way I always do, at these images, so far removed from the familiar clichés, my thoughts turn to the beautiful women he immortalized. Photographs fix the fleeting, immortalize the ephemeral. Many of the women Jonvelle photographed are now old or dead, but – thanks to this photographer who is now also dead – their perfection will never fade.

Every one of Jonvelle’s photographs is a declaration of love. One day, at my request, he photographed Delphine Vallette, the mother of my daughter. I wanted to give this brunette whom I loved a portrait. Never have I felt such a cuckold – though in the most erotic of ways.

Beauty is an evanescent mystery that some artists have the ability to capture. As I look again at these wonderful images, I’m reminded of the title of that American comedy Drop Dead Gorgeous. Jonvelle’s work as a whole is not an ode to femininity; the story it tells is of the battle to vanquish death by means of the celebration of desire. All these shoulders caught by surprise, these half-seen breasts, these finely- arched insteps, these flawless backs, this sensual solitude, this calm between two storms, all these beautiful women who don’t give a damn are simply doors softly opened, through which we may catch a glimpse of eternal life.

Frédéric Beigbeder

Jean-François Jonvelle was born in 1943 in Cavaillon, south of France. Soon he will sell famous melons to buy Hasselblad. Its inspirations will come from the painting of Balthus, Bacon, of Schiele, but the true influence comes from films from Mankiewicz, Lubitsch, Fritz Lang, Orson Welles, Arthur PEN, Minnelli and more recently of Terry Gillian of which it acknowledges to have seen eleven times the film Brazil ; Finally its preferred film: Jules and Jim of François Truffaut.

In 1959, it is the photographer George Glasberg who initiates him with photography while making him make the turn of France of the cathedrals. It is a photographic revelation which will leave it never again.

At the age of 20 he becomes the assistant of the American photographer Richard Avedon. After this enriching experiment he becomes his own “Master” whose favorite subject will be the woman. Her mom and her small sister of whom he always was very near will be her “first agreeing victims”. Then come the first “muse” and accomplice, Tina Sportolaro whom he meets in 1982 and with which he carries out some of his more beautiful images. Will be then Béatrice, Myriam and many others …

He is in particular the author of the photographs of the pub campaign which had revolutionized the advertising display in the Eighties “Tomorrow I remove bottom”.

He published many books; some of which are: in 1983: Those which I Like ; 1989 Jonvelle (s) 1994: April, May, June ; 1996: Mad of them ; 1998: Balconies . An important monograph will be published in 2011.

Jonvelle said readily that its preferred subject was the woman that it liked. “When I photograph a woman said he, I want that she knows that she is most beautiful on earth, because a woman who feel beautiful becomes really the most beautiful woman. My happiness, it is also never not to have puted in chains my freedom, nor lost my freshness, my perfect moment”.

Jean François left us on January 16, 2002

editorial_title_zh: 哥伦比亚国家博物馆因移除LGBTQ与女性主义展品爆发抗议
editorial_excerpt_zh: 此次撤展源于总统阿韦拉尔多·德拉埃斯普里耶拉针对所谓“觉醒主义”（wokismo）的右翼竞选活动。

article_text:
Protesters assembled around Bogota’s National Museum of Colombia over the weekend after the removal of more than 30 objects “related to the struggles of the LGBTQ+ movement, feminism, and the political left,” according to the digital news source Colombia One .

As reported , “The decision by Abelardo De La Espriella’s government, announced last Friday, turned the area around the museum into a site of public demonstrations against what protesters describe as ‘an attempt to impose an ideological view of the country’s history.’”

The protests on Saturday and Sunday included anti-censorship sentiment and political theater but also clashes with the police, who used water cannons and riot-control equipment to combat opponents of De La Espriella’s right-wing campaign against so-called wokismo .

“Some participants placed reproductions of the removed works outside the museum, bringing them back into the public space and denouncing their disappearance from the exhibitions as an attempt to silence the stories they represented,” according to Colombia One . “The affected materials included objects and documents related to feminist and LGBTQ+ causes, the history of Colombia’s political left, and the 2016 peace agreement with the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).”

The National Museum has not posted anything related to the protests to its website or social media accounts, but the former does include a notice dated October 6 about damage done to Fernando Botero’s bronze sculpture The Dove of Peace . After a visitor knocked over the work while leaning against its pedestal to take a photograph, the museum’s conservation department found abrasions and a loss of paint as well as “dents in the metal, resulting from the impact on different points of the sculpture, especially the beak.”
excerpt_original: The banishment owes to president Abelardo De La Espriella’s right-wing campaign against so-called wokismo.

article_text:
Outerlight Entertainment , formerly known as First Look Entertainment, has acquired feature independent studio Bleecker Street Media.

Currently, Bleecker Street has the critically acclaimed Alex Gibney directed documentary Musk in release, about SpaceX and Tesla boss Elon Musk.

Founded in 2014 by the late film executive Andrew Karpen, Bleecker Street has built itself into a library counting close to one hundred titles. Bleecker Street will continue to be led by its current CEO Kent Sanderson, who took over the auteur distribution label following Karpen’s passing. Chief Marketing Officer Tyler DiNapoli will also remain at Bleecker following the acquisition.

Related Stories

Guy Nattiv & Carrie Coon On Finding Empathy In 'The Liberation': "Who Are We To Say What Is Required For Someone To Move On?" - Contenders London

'Musk' Director Alex Gibney On World's Richest Man: "He's A Bullsh*tter"

Bleecker Street will continue to manage its own slate, acquisitions, distribution strategy, marketing, filmmaker relationships and day-to-day operations. With the backing of Outerlight, Bleecker Street plans to increase its investment in its existing film business while expanding new growth initiatives, including sister cinema event label Crosswalk. With its new owner, it’s business as usual for Bleecker Street: They will remain an active buyer and distributor in the indie sphere, and their current slate and existing commitments will continue without disruption.

Watch on Deadline

Outerlight’s purchase of Bleecker will provide the distributor with long-term capital and additional resources for growth. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. Bleecker Street Media was advised on the transaction by Sandy Climan of Entertainment Media Ventures and Matthew Wilkens of 44 Greenwich. Pryor Cashman represented Outerlight Entertainment on the transaction.

“Bleecker Street is growing, and our ambition is to continue scaling the company while staying true to what has always made us distinctive, said Sanderson. “Outerlight shares our belief in the power of cinema and the importance of theatrical moviegoing, and its long-term backing gives us additional capacity to pursue the opportunities we see across our core film business as well as compelling new avenues in the film space. We’re excited about what we can build from here.”

Outerlight’s portfolio includes such companies as Topic Studios, Bleecker Street, and Puzzle Pictures, along with investments in MHz Choice and Passionflix, plus other targeted investments and joint ventures.

Bleecker’s other fall theatrical releases include Anton Corbijn’s A Talent for Murder , starring Helen Mirren; Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care, starring Kate O’Flynn; Zachary Wigon’s Victorian Psycho starring Maika Monroe; and Guy Nattiv’s The Liberation , starring Carrie Coon, Lily James, Odessa Young, Tracy Letts and Bella Ramsey. Crosswalk recently released Hadestown: The Musical , which grossed more than $20 million stateside during its limited theatrical run and became the highest-grossing live theater capture to date. It also released concert film Stray Kids: The DominATE Experience earlier in the year, which was the No. 1 movie at the global B.O. upon its opening weekend. Crosswalk has George Michael: The Faith Tour opening in December.

"当我还是个孩子的时候，我从来不想拥有一个花园……我远比除草更喜欢艺术，用我最喜欢的2支蜡笔——砖红色和森林绿色进行涂色。我在空白纸张上画花，并将它们“种”在我卧室的墙壁上。我想用艺术覆盖我的墙壁——不一定是很漂亮的花，而是那些能对我诉说的花——生气的花、悲伤的花、快乐的花。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "开展我的花卉项目是一次对童年玩乐和创造乐趣的回归。《花之道》探讨了我对花卉表现潜力的持续迷恋，这种联系可以追溯到我童年的蜡笔画。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": article_text:
Piper Smith: The Way of Flowers

©Piper Smith, Reflection

I first met Piper Smith at Review Santa Fe last year. She showed me a number of works, from everyday objects in New York City to flower portraits, each one was slightly obscured. We had a wonderful conversation and I have kept up with her work since. I thought of her work, The Way of Flowers, the other day while I was teaching in Art History. We were discussing Plato’s Theory of Forms and using the idea of beauty, I asked students to give me an example of the imitation of beauty and most thought of flowers. I see this exploration in Smith’s series, exploring the variations of expression that flowers hold.

©Piper Smith, Day and Night

Piper Smith is a Hell’s Kitchen, NYC-based fine art photographer specializing in abstract compositions. Her artistic journey began with a BFA from the Goodman Theater School of Drama in Chicago, followed by a successful career as a stage actor and commercial spokesperson. Transitioning to represent and work with illustrators ignited her passion for photography, leading her to studies at ICP, SVA, and Parsons. She continues to refine her craft under Christopher Giglio’s THE GRAMMAR OF PHOTOGRAPHY, a program she likens to her graduate studies. Piper’s previous work has been showcased in numerous national and international exhibitions, including the 1650 Gallery, followed by Jadite Gallery, Hobart Gallery, The Pleiades Gallery, Viridian Artists, Praxis Gallery, PhotoPlace, Soho Photo Gallery, Hudson Guild, Grey Cube and the BW Athens Photography International Exhibition in 2023. She was also part of the 6th Development Program at BH Photo.

Follow Piper on Instagram: @pipersmithny

©Piper Smith, Wind Swept

The Way of Flowers

When I was a child, I never wanted a garden… I much preferred Art to Weeding, coloring with my 2 favorite crayons, the brick red and the forest green. I drew flowers on blank pieces of paper and “planted” them on my bedroom walls. I wanted to cover my walls with art – not necessarily pretty flowers but flowers that spoke to me – angry flowers, sad flowers, cheerful flowers.

The unexpected stillness of the Covid-19 pandemic echoed the self-contained world of my childhood artmaking. Turning my attention to the real flowers that arrived with grocery deliveries, I rediscovered the profound joy of experimenting with color, backgrounds, and composition. Printing these photographs and arranging them in my studio evoked the same sense I experienced as a child “planting” my walls with crayon drawings. The magic is seeing the flower in your mind’s eye, the excitement of the beginning. The science is standing back and thinking how to make it real, how to get the long stem to balance on the candlestick.

Working with my flower project is a return to childhood play and the pleasure of invention. “The Way of Flowers” explores my ongoing fascination with the expressive potential of a flower, a connection that traces back to my childhood crayon drawings.

©Piper Smith, Solitaire

Epiphany Knedler: How did your project come about?

Piper Smith: The Way of Flowers really came out of something I started doing during the pandemic. I’d walk to Central Park, find a tree set apart from the others, and walk around it a few times, shooting from different angles. Back in the studio I’d layer those angles together in Photoshop, keeping the different viewpoints faintly visible, and then play around with color. That’s how Ghost Tree came about.

©Piper Smith, Ghost Tree

After about thirty trees, a friend challenged me to change direction, so I set up a small studio in my NYC apartment and did the same thing with a flower instead—rotated it, shot it from different angles, and was pleasantly surprised by what I got. That one became Ethereal, and it turned into The Way of Flowers, a project that ended up taking me well over a year to shoot. Friends lent me all kinds of unusual vases and containers, and Whole Foods turned out to have a great variety of flowers.

©Piper Smith, Ethereal

EK: Is there a specific image that is your favorite or particularly meaningful to this series?

PS: Three is still my favorite, and it’s the one that’s gone on to win awards. It’s a tiny ceramic vase, barely an inch tall, with one slender stem in it. I shot it from a bunch of angles like I always do, then picked three of those frames and merged them into one image. There’s something about how minimal it is—just balance and line and quiet—that feels like the purest version of what I was going for with the whole series.

©Piper Smith, Three

EK: Can you tell us about your artistic practice?

PS: My practice comes down to experimentation and a real love for the print. I don’t think of a photograph as one single moment—I’m circling something, gathering angles, and building those layers back together, so what you end up with feels more like a sculpture of a subject than a snapshot of it.

Once I finished The Way of Flowers , I started walking through my neighborhood, Hell’s Kitchen, with my camera—shooting skyscrapers, parking signs, and a mannequin in a store window. I had a feeling of not being able to get out of there… it was a dark canyon with brightly lit buildings above—it felt like there was NO EXIT ! That became No Exit .

Then a trip to Greenland pushed things further—I was shooting icebergs from a RIB boat, close enough to taste the ice. Not long after, I was in the high desert outside Santa Fe shooting lava mountains, hoodoos, and buttes. I started noticing how close those two landscapes were to each other, even though ice and lava seem like opposites, and that’s turned into my next project, Grounding Truth.

©Piper Smith, Ghosting

EK: What’s next for you?

PS: I’ve got a busy fall coming up! End of August I leave for Portugal for a few weeks to shoot open-air markets, the vibrant neighborhoods of Cais do Sodré and Bairro Alto in old Lisbon, and traditional Mercados de Ciganos.

Following that trip, I have two shows featuring work from No Exit : a feature exhibition opening October 8th at Soho Photo Gallery (539 W 23rd St, New York, NY), and a group show opening October 17th at FOMA in Santa Fe.

And I should mention—I was born and raised in the Midwest, Inver Grove Heights, Minnesota!

©Piper Smith, Her Lips

©Piper Smith, Jester

©Piper Smith, Caged

©Piper Smith, Metallica

©Piper Smith, Side Step

©Piper Smith, Tick Tock

©Piper Smith, Prayer

©Piper Smith, Pure Love

Epiphany Knedler is an interdisciplinary artist + educator exploring the ways we engage with history. She graduated from the University of South Dakota with a BFA in Studio Art and a BA in Political Science and completed her MFA in Studio Art at East Carolina University. She is based in Aberdeen, South Dakota, serving as an Assistant Professor of Art and Chair of the Art Department at Northern State University, a Content Editor with LENSCRATCH, and the co-founder and curator of the art collective Midwest Nice Art. Her work has been exhibited in the New York Times, the Guardian, Vermont Center for Photography, Lenscratch, Dek Unu Arts, and awarded through Lensculture, the Lucie Foundation, F-Stop Magazine, and Photolucida Critical Mass.

Follow Epiphany on Instagram: @epiphanysk

article_text:
As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt , the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and filmmakers turned to what the industry needs to turn its wealth of talent into films that can find audiences both at home and abroad.

Egyptian cinema once dominated film production across the Arab world, but output fell dramatically from its late-20th-century heights. According to figures from the Egyptian Chamber of Cinema Industry, the country produced 112 films in 1988, before output fell to just 16 a decade later. More recently, production has shown signs of recovery, rising from 51 feature films in 2022 to 67 in 2023.

Related Stories

Raj Singh and Italy's RP1 Holding Launch €100 Million Film Fund to Boost Country's Struggling Indie Ecosystem

‘Star Trek’ 60th Anniversary Celebration Hits Rome MIA Market With Iconic Franchise at 'Crossroads’ After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger

For veteran Syrian producer Mohamed Mashish , who has built a decades-long career in Egypt, capitalizing on that momentum starts with the screenplay.

Popular on Variety

“We need to have more time for development and scriptwriting,” he tells Variety . “We have all the industry components. But we don’t have scripts. So what can you do? I have a nice camera, a good DP, but we can’t do anything without good scripts.”

Mashish has seen firsthand how new platforms can expand the reach of Egyptian storytelling. He produced the 2016 drama “Grand Hotel,” which became the first Egyptian and first Arabic-language series to land on Netflix when the streamer released it internationally as “Secret of the Nile” in 2018.

He believes younger filmmakers are also benefiting from greater access to work from around the world. “They’re more open-minded. They’re connected on the internet and everything,” he notes. “Because the platforms are available now, they’re watching more than just our culture. So they are more open and they are ready to move.”

But Mashish argues that new perspectives need to be matched with experience. “We have to bring the old generation and the new generation together,” he explains. “The new generation brings a different perspective, but cinema still needs experience, so we need to combine that new talent with the expertise that already exists in the industry.”

Egyptian director Hadi El Bagoury , whose 2016 “Hepta: The Last Lecture” became the highest-grossing romantic film in Egyptian cinema, points to streaming as one of the biggest opportunities for homegrown talent.

The growth of platforms, he argues, has given filmmakers more places to show their work while exposing audiences to a wider range of filmmaking. “You discover new stories, new directors, new genres,” he says. “You discover a lot more directors, DPs, actors and different styles.”

That exposure is also changing what audiences expect from Egyptian cinema. “They want new genres, they want original stories,” El Bagoury says.

The shift has particular consequences in the Gulf, a crucial market for Egyptian films. Mashish points to Saudi Arabia’s theatrical expansion as an example of how quickly audiences have evolved.

“At the beginning, when the Saudis started to open cinemas, they accepted everything because it was new,” he recalls. “It’s like, ‘I will go to the cinema, I will have popcorn, no matter the kind of movie I will watch.'”

“They are more selective than before,” he continues. “They will not accept just anything coming anymore. Because cinemas are now open in Saudi and in the Gulf, they are watching international cinema. So they demand this kind of quality.”

For Lebanese producer and distributor Ziad Srouji (“ Palestine 36 ”), whose career spans film and television across the Arab world, reaching audiences beyond the region does not mean making Arab films resemble foreign ones.

“Specificity travels; generic does not,” he stresses. “International buyers aren’t looking for Arab films that imitate Western genre cinema, and they’re tired of films made only to explain the region to outsiders. They want stories rooted in a very particular world but driven by a premise anyone can grasp in one sentence.”

For Srouji, the challenges often come after the initial idea. “A good idea gets you into the room. It doesn’t get you through production, and it certainly doesn’t get you to an audience.”

The bigger obstacles, he believes, are often structural. “Too many films reach the market without a sales agent attached early, without delivery materials ready and without a positioning strategy beyond a festival premiere,” Srouji says. “Sales and distribution need a strategy built from day one, not after the premiere.”

El Gouna is among the regional festivals trying to strengthen the path from development onward. CineGouna, its industry arm, launched the Egyptian Voices strand this year, selecting four Egyptian projects in development for tailored training in pitching, packaging and co-production.

El Bagoury argues that the industry also needs more ways to reach audiences directly. “We need more Egyptian-owned platforms, more theaters. Theaters that are cheap, accessible to all,” he says. “We need a lot of this so we don’t have to depend on anybody else. We need to show our films in our cinemas and on our platforms.”

For Srouji, the ultimate measure of a healthy industry is not simply whether a filmmaker gets a movie made or lands a prestigious festival selection, but whether that success makes the next film possible.

“A major festival selection is a launch, not a career,” he says. “Sustainable success is when your second film is easier to finance than your first.”

excerpt_original: As the ninth edition of El Gouna Film Festival wrapped in Egypt, the conversation among some of the country’s and region’s leading producers and filmmakers turned to what the industry needs to turn its wealth of talent into films that can find audiences both at home and abroad.…

translated_excerpt_zh: 在埃及举行的第九届El Gouna电影节时,一些国家和地区领先的制片人和电影制作人之间的对话转向了行业需要将其丰富的天赋转化为能够在国内外找到观众的电影。
